(b) Every day, Californians are also facing an
affordability crisis. Costs for housing, food, electricity,
health care, home and auto insurance, and many other
life necessities continue to escalate. Californians are
struggling economically just to make ends meet on a
daily basis. Saving for retirement or a rainy day is even
harder. Given the state’s extraordinarily high cost of
living, a recent analysis suggests that Californians
would need $2.3 million saved up if they want to retire
comfortably for 20 years. This is an impossible sum for
many Californians.
(c) To make matters worse, politicians and special
interest groups want to start taxing retirement holdings,
individually owned assets, and other forms of personal
savings—even though the “California Dream” is getting
further out of reach for many of us and many
Californians struggle to save enough money to retire.
Here is just some of what could be at risk:
(1) Teachers, police officers, firefighters, and other
dedicated workers earn defined-benefit pension
benefits. They could be taxed on the future value of
their pension benefits and forced to pay the
government before they ever collect a dime in pension
pay.
(2) Californians who contribute to 401(k) retirement
plans and individual retirement accounts (IRAs), and
invest in stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and other
investments could be taxed on the value of their
retirement nest eggs. This could cost workers some of
their hard-earned savings, causing them to put off
retirement and leaving them more economically
vulnerable later in life.
(d) California already imposes income taxes, capital
gains taxes, real property taxes, personal property
taxes, corporation taxes, sales and use taxes, real
property transaction taxes and many other taxes on its
residents. In addition, once Californians begin to
access their retirement holdings, sell their individually
owned assets, or realize the growth in other personal
savings, they are already subject to the state’s income,
capital gains, and property taxes. But politicians and
special interests should be prohibited from taxing the
mere ownership or control of personal property such as
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings that Californians work
hard to save.
(e) Retroactive taxes can have the same devastating
effects on Californians’ retirement planning and
personal savings. Fundamental principles of fairness in
a democratic society require that individuals, families,
and businesses be able to understand and rely upon
the tax laws that govern their financial planning so they
can make decisions with advance notice of what the
rules are.
(f) The ability of Californians to organize and achieve
their financial and retirement goals depends on having
advance notice of the tax obligations that apply to
them. Retroactive changes to tax laws are
fundamentally unfair and undermine confidence in
government, disrupt retirement and financial planning,
and prevent residents and businesses from preparing
for the future.
(g) Sacramento politicians and special interests have
wasted billions of our tax dollars on inefficient and
ineffective programs. But they keep coming back for
more of our money with more tax proposals. They don’t
need to tax our retirement holdings or tax us
retroactively based on past conduct, activities, or
status—they need to deliver better results with what
taxpayers have already given them to spend.
SEC. 3. Statement of Purpose.
In enacting this act, the purpose and intent of the
people of the State of California is to protect
Californians’ ability to save for their futures by
prohibiting the imposition of new taxes on our personal
property, including the ownership or control of
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings as well as requiring all
new taxes to only apply prospectively.

SECTION 1. Prohibition on Taxing Retirement Holdings,

(a) No state law and no provision of this Constitution

taxation of real property as provided in other provisions

present prior to the effective date of the state law or
constitutional provision.

on a taxpayer based upon their residency status on a
date prior to the effective date of the tax.

imposition or collection of any tax that was in effect,
imposed, and first collected on or before December 31,
2025.

living, a recent analysis suggests that Californians
would need $2.3 million saved up if they want to retire
comfortably for 20 years. This is an impossible sum for
many Californians.
(c) To make matters worse, politicians and special
interest groups want to start taxing retirement holdings,
individually owned assets, and other forms of personal
savings—even though the “California Dream” is getting
further out of reach for many of us and many
Californians struggle to save enough money to retire.
Here is just some of what could be at risk:
(1) Teachers, police officers, firefighters, and other
dedicated workers earn defined-benefit pension
benefits. They could be taxed on the future value of
their pension benefits and forced to pay the
government before they ever collect a dime in pension
pay.
(2) Californians who contribute to 401(k) retirement
plans and individual retirement accounts (IRAs), and
invest in stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and other
investments could be taxed on the value of their
retirement nest eggs. This could cost workers some of
their hard-earned savings, causing them to put off
retirement and leaving them more economically
vulnerable later in life.
(d) California already imposes income taxes, capital
gains taxes, real property taxes, personal property
taxes, corporation taxes, sales and use taxes, real
property transaction taxes and many other taxes on its
residents. In addition, once Californians begin to
access their retirement holdings, sell their individually
owned assets, or realize the growth in other personal
savings, they are already subject to the state’s income,
capital gains, and property taxes. But politicians and
special interests should be prohibited from taxing the
mere ownership or control of personal property such as
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings that Californians work
hard to save.
(e) Retroactive taxes can have the same devastating
effects on Californians’ retirement planning and
personal savings. Fundamental principles of fairness in
a democratic society require that individuals, families,
and businesses be able to understand and rely upon
the tax laws that govern their financial planning so they
can make decisions with advance notice of what the
rules are.
(f) The ability of Californians to organize and achieve
their financial and retirement goals depends on having
advance notice of the tax obligations that apply to
them. Retroactive changes to tax laws are
fundamentally unfair and undermine confidence in
government, disrupt retirement and financial planning,
and prevent residents and businesses from preparing
for the future.
(g) Sacramento politicians and special interests have
wasted billions of our tax dollars on inefficient and
ineffective programs. But they keep coming back for
more of our money with more tax proposals. They don’t
need to tax our retirement holdings or tax us
retroactively based on past conduct, activities, or
status—they need to deliver better results with what
taxpayers have already given them to spend.
SEC. 3. Statement of Purpose.
In enacting this act, the purpose and intent of the
people of the State of California is to protect
Californians’ ability to save for their futures by
prohibiting the imposition of new taxes on our personal
property, including the ownership or control of
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings as well as requiring all
new taxes to only apply prospectively.
SEC. 4. Article VIII is added to the California
Constitution, to read:
ARTICLE VIII
SECTION 1. Prohibition on Taxing Retirement Holdings,
Individually Owned Assets, and Other Forms of Personal
Savings
(a) No state law and no provision of this Constitution
enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may enact, create,
impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership
or control of retirement holdings, individually owned
assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether
held directly or indirectly.
(b) Nothing in this section shall alter or limit the
imposition or collection of any tax that was in effect,
imposed, and first collected on or before December 31,
2025.
(c) Nothing in this section shall alter or affect the
taxation of real property as provided in other provisions
of this Constitution.
SEC. 2. Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
(a) (1) No state law and no provision of this
Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may
enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax
that operates retroactively to result in tax liability based
on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred or was
present prior to the effective date of the state law or
constitutional provision.
(2) This subdivision also applies to a tax that is imposed
on a taxpayer based upon their residency status on a
date prior to the effective date of the tax.
(b) Nothing in subdivision (a) shall alter or limit the
imposition or collection of any tax that was in effect,
imposed, and first collected on or before December 31,
2025.

investment accounts, business interests, digital assets,

Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on a California resident taxpayer’s covered net assets exceeding $1 billion.
Although the tax is limited to California residents, the residency determination is made as of Jan. 1, 2026.
Unlike an individual income tax, which generally applies to income earned or received during a taxable period, the proposed tax would apply to accumulated net wealth measured by reference to the value of the taxpayer’s covered assets, less specified liabilities.
The proposed tax base would encompass a broad range of assets, including:
- Publicly traded stocks and other marketable securities;
- Stock and other ownership interests in privately held businesses;
- Partnership and limited liability company interests;
- Venture capital and private equity investments;
- Intellectual property, including patents, trademarks, copyrights and similar intangible assets;
- Trust and beneficial ownership interests;
- Art, collectibles and other investment property (subject to the exclusions described below); and

SEC. 5. This article applies to all statewide initiative
measures submitted to the electors on or after
January 1, 2026, including measures that appear on

adding this article is approved by the electors.
SEC. 5. Conflicting Measures.
(a) (1) In the event that this initiative measure appears
on the same statewide election ballot as another
initiative measure that (A) imposes different audit rules
on special taxes; or (B) contains a state tax that is
exempted or excluded from the Government Spending
Limitation, then that other initiative measure shall be
deemed to be in conflict with this measure. In the event
that this initiative measure receives a greater number
of affirmative votes, the provisions of this measure shall
prevail in their entirety, and all the provisions of the
other measure shall be null and void.
(2) For purposes of this section, “special tax” shall
have the same meaning as set forth in Section 4 of this
act.
(b) If this initiative measure is approved by the voters
but superseded in whole or in part by any other
conflicting initiative measure approved by the voters at
the same election, and such conflicting measure is
later held invalid, this measure shall be self-executing
and given full force and effect.
SEC. 6. Severability.
The provisions of this act are severable. If any portion,
section, subdivision, paragraph, clause, subclause,
sentence, phrase, word, or application of this act is for
any reason held to be invalid by a decision of any court
of competent jurisdiction, that decision shall not affect
the validity of the remaining portions of this act. The
people of the State of California hereby declare that
they would have adopted this act and each and every
portion, section, subdivision, paragraph, clause,
subclause, sentence, phrase, word, and application not
declared invalid or unconstitutional without regard to
whether any part of this act or application thereof
would be subsequently declared invalid.

SEC. 8. Liberal Construction.
This act shall be liberally construed to give effect to its

The purpose of this section is to ensure that the

approved by the voters of the State of California and

General refuse to defend this act to the fullest extent
possible on behalf of the State of California, then the
following actions shall be taken:
(a) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained
in Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 12500) of Part

other law, the Attorney General shall appoint
independent counsel to faithfully and vigorously defend
this act to the fullest extent possible on behalf of the
State of California.
(b) Before appointing or thereafter substituting
independent counsel, the Attorney General shall
exercise due diligence in determining the qualifications
of independent counsel and shall obtain written
affirmation from independent counsel that independent
counsel will faithfully and vigorously defend this act to
the fullest extent possible. The written affirmation shall
be made publicly available immediately upon request.
(c) In order to support the defense of this act in
instances where the Governor and Attorney General fail
to do so despite the will of the voters, a continuous
appropriation is hereby made from the General Fund to
the Controller, without regard to fiscal years, in an
amount necessary to cover the costs of retaining
independent counsel to faithfully and vigorously defend
this act on behalf of the State of California to the fullest
extent possible.
PROPOSITION 42
This initiative measure is submitted to the people in
accordance with the provisions of Section 8 of Article II
of the California Constitution.
This initiative measure adds sections to the California
Constitution; therefore, new provisions proposed to be
added are printed in italic type to indicate that they are
new.
PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the
Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of
2026.
SEC. 2. Findings and Declarations.
(a) California families are paying more for everything
and we already pay some of the highest taxes in the
country. A recent analysis by a nonpartisan research
institute concluded that California ranks 3rd worst in
the nation in subjecting its population to taxes when
considering individual income taxes, sales taxes,
property taxes, and other forms of taxation. California is
behind only New Jersey and the District of Columbia in
this regard. California also has the highest state sales
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 42 CONTINUED
tax in the nation, the highest top income tax rate, and
the highest tax on gasoline, among other indicators.
(b) Every day, Californians are also facing an
affordability crisis. Costs for housing, food, electricity,
health care, home and auto insurance, and many other
life necessities continue to escalate. Californians are
struggling economically just to make ends meet on a
daily basis. Saving for retirement or a rainy day is even
harder. Given the state’s extraordinarily high cost of
living, a recent analysis suggests that Californians
would need $2.3 million saved up if they want to retire
comfortably for 20 years. This is an impossible sum for
many Californians.
(c) To make matters worse, politicians and special
interest groups want to start taxing retirement holdings,
individually owned assets, and other forms of personal
savings—even though the “California Dream” is getting
further out of reach for many of us and many
Californians struggle to save enough money to retire.
Here is just some of what could be at risk:
(1) Teachers, police officers, firefighters, and other
dedicated workers earn defined-benefit pension
benefits. They could be taxed on the future value of
their pension benefits and forced to pay the
government before they ever collect a dime in pension
pay.
(2) Californians who contribute to 401(k) retirement
plans and individual retirement accounts (IRAs), and
invest in stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and other
investments could be taxed on the value of their
retirement nest eggs. This could cost workers some of
their hard-earned savings, causing them to put off
retirement and leaving them more economically
vulnerable later in life.
(d) California already imposes income taxes, capital
gains taxes, real property taxes, personal property
taxes, corporation taxes, sales and use taxes, real
property transaction taxes and many other taxes on its
residents. In addition, once Californians begin to
access their retirement holdings, sell their individually
owned assets, or realize the growth in other personal
savings, they are already subject to the state’s income,
capital gains, and property taxes. But politicians and
special interests should be prohibited from taxing the
mere ownership or control of personal property such as
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings that Californians work
hard to save.
(e) Retroactive taxes can have the same devastating
effects on Californians’ retirement planning and
personal savings. Fundamental principles of fairness in
a democratic society require that individuals, families,
and businesses be able to understand and rely upon
the tax laws that govern their financial planning so they
can make decisions with advance notice of what the
rules are.
(f) The ability of Californians to organize and achieve
their financial and retirement goals depends on having
advance notice of the tax obligations that apply to
them. Retroactive changes to tax laws are
fundamentally unfair and undermine confidence in
government, disrupt retirement and financial planning,
and prevent residents and businesses from preparing
for the future.
(g) Sacramento politicians and special interests have
wasted billions of our tax dollars on inefficient and
ineffective programs. But they keep coming back for
more of our money with more tax proposals. They don’t
need to tax our retirement holdings or tax us
retroactively based on past conduct, activities, or
status—they need to deliver better results with what
taxpayers have already given them to spend.
SEC. 3. Statement of Purpose.
In enacting this act, the purpose and intent of the
people of the State of California is to protect
Californians’ ability to save for their futures by
prohibiting the imposition of new taxes on our personal
property, including the ownership or control of
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings as well as requiring all
new taxes to only apply prospectively.
SEC. 4. Article VIII is added to the California
Constitution, to read:
ARTICLE VIII
SECTION 1. Prohibition on Taxing Retirement Holdings,
Individually Owned Assets, and Other Forms of Personal
Savings
(a) No state law and no provision of this Constitution
enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may enact, create,
impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership
or control of retirement holdings, individually owned
assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether
held directly or indirectly.
(b) Nothing in this section shall alter or limit the
imposition or collection of any tax that was in effect,
imposed, and first collected on or before December 31,
2025.
(c) Nothing in this section shall alter or affect the
taxation of real property as provided in other provisions
of this Constitution.
SEC. 2. Prohibition on Retroactive Taxes
(a) (1) No state law and no provision of this
Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may
enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax
that operates retroactively to result in tax liability based
on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred or was

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Carefully reviewing the proposition details to form a recommendation.

Prop 42 would ban new state taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and personal savings starting January 1, 2026. The definition is extremely broad.

The definition covers pensions, 401(k)s, IRAs, mutual funds, and all personal property including digital assets, business interests, and intellectual property.

The proposition also prohibits retroactive taxes with limited exceptions for emergencies. Taxes in effect before December 31, 2025 remain unchanged. Real property taxation is unaffected.

Prop 42 contains a conflict clause. If it passes with more votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 is null and void entirely.

The campaign frames this as protecting middle-class retirement from double taxation. However, California currently does not tax ownership of retirement accounts or financial assets. No serious legislative proposal exists that would tax ordinary 401(k)s.

The proposition is funded by billionaire donors, including Sergey Brin, and its main purpose appears to be killing Prop 40. Major editorial boards have called it a poison pill and decoy.

Its broad definition would also constitutionally block future wealth taxes and taxes on business interests, intellectual property, digital assets, and personal belongings.

The ban would be permanent, requiring a constitutional amendment to undo it.

The retroactivity prohibition is broader than the retirement protection. It would generally bar retroactive taxes with only narrow emergency exceptions.

Prop 40 already exempts qualified retirement accounts and limits Roth conversions to $10 million. The warning about 401(k) taxes is therefore largely false.

The broad constitutional prohibition would add another rigid constraint on California's tax system. This reduces flexibility for future crises such as climate change, healthcare needs, or AI economic disruption.

The Mercury News specifically warns that the proposition would "senselessly shackles the state's fiscal future" in the face of AI-induced economic uncertainties.

Local taxes remain unaffected. Vehicle license fees and existing personal property taxes continue.

Arguments for Prop 42 independent of Prop 40 include the difficulty of valuing private businesses, art, and intellectual property. Wealth taxes would be litigation-prone. Some billionaires have already left California, suggesting capital flight.

European countries largely repealed wealth taxes due to capital flight, administrative costs, and low revenue. Taxing unrealized gains can force sales of illiquid assets. Wealth already taxed as income creates legitimate double taxation concerns. California already imposes the highest top income tax rate in the United States plus high capital gains taxes.

Prop 40 would tax people based on residency as of January 1, 2026. This is genuinely retroactive and punitive because it cannot be avoided by leaving after the measure qualifies.

Constitutional protection of savings from wealth taxation is a legitimate policy preference. Many voters reasonably do not want the state to have the power to tax asset ownership.

The slippery slope argument is not always fallacious in tax policy. Opening the door to wealth taxes could allow future expansions beyond billionaires, similar to how income tax and AMT evolved. Supporters cite six proposals targeting retirement and savings, but these claims need verification. The Orange County Register and San Bernardino Sun have endorsed YES on both propositions specifically to limit taxation.

Pension unions representing firefighters, building trades, and peace officers support Prop 42. The healthcare union SEIU-UHW supports Prop 40 instead. These pension unions fear future expansions of wealth taxes despite the current exemptions.

California's budget depends heavily on high-income taxpayers and capital gains. Blocking wealth taxes could protect that revenue base from flight.

Voting YES on Prop 42 is effectively voting to kill Prop 40. If you oppose the billionaire tax, vote directly on Prop 40 instead of allowing a misleading measure to nullify it.

The constitutional ban would also permanently block future non-retroactive wealth taxes and taxes on digital assets.

The conflict clause is especially problematic. It would void an entire competing measure, even parts that do not actually conflict with Prop 42.

A blanket constitutional ban also prevents future voters from rejecting specific bad proposals without undoing the entire tax system.

The broad definition could also block new vehicle taxes, state-level business personal property taxes, and taxes on unrealized capital gains if structured as ownership or control taxes.

The definition of "tax" in Prop 42 is drawn from Article XIII A Section 3. That section was broadened by Prop 26 in 2010 to cover any state levy, charge, or exaction. Fees that are not technically taxes may still be permitted.

The Mercury News and San Francisco Chronicle both recommend voting NO on Prop 42. I still need to verify the six retirement tax proposals and review the LAO analysis of Prop 40 before finalizing a recommendation.

The Sacramento Bee also recommends voting NO on Prop 42. The editorial consensus is largely against it, even among papers that oppose Prop 40.

I am weighing whether to rely on that consensus or form my own independent view. I generally oppose broad constitutional tax prohibitions that lock in policy beyond the specific problem. California's experience with Prop 13 offers a cautionary tale about how popular constitutional limits can create long-term structural problems.

The proposition's marketing is dishonest. It frames itself as a simple 401(k) protection, but the actual text bans ownership taxes on nearly all non-real-estate property and includes a broad retroactivity clause. A blanket constitutional ban is also too sweeping; voting no on Prop 40 would address the specific retroactive billionaire tax without destroying the state's fiscal flexibility.

The LAO analysis confirms that voting no on Prop 42 leaves the state free to consider future wealth tax proposals on their merits. It does not guarantee that such taxes will be adopted.

The fear of future middle-class retirement taxes is weak. Political incentives strongly protect 401(k)s and pensions. The pension unions supporting Prop 42 may be aligned with the billionaire PAC funding. Their support should be checked for independence. Billionaire funding does not automatically make a policy bad. Skepticism is warranted when the public justification does not match the operative effect and the primary funders' interests.

Estate taxes are typically transfer taxes rather than ownership taxes, so they likely would not be blocked. The recommendation is NO, but I am now carefully weighing the YES side to ensure a balanced analysis.

The opposition to Prop 40 is broader than billionaire PAC funding. California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, school boards, and primary care groups all oppose it. Many Democrats and healthcare organizations are against the measure. The SEIU-UHW union placed a poorly designed retroactive wealth tax on the ballot to fund its industry.

Polls showed Prop 40 was competitive, so a constitutional backstop may be the only reliable way to stop a harmful tax if voters are confused by multiple measures. Wealth taxes are almost uniformly considered bad policy by tax economists across the political spectrum.

France's wealth tax illustrates how thresholds creep downward once a tax exists. A constitutional ban is a credible commitment against that drift.

Retroactive taxation based on a pre-election residency date sets a dangerous precedent. Future initiatives could trap voters who cannot leave the state in time.

A constitutional ban on retroactive taxes is a rule-of-law protection that benefits everyone, not just billionaires. Keeping bad options open is not inherently democratic wisdom; constitutions exist precisely to take some options off the table. A stable rule against wealth-taxing middle-class savings also protects ordinary savers.

Existing taxes on vehicles and business equipment are grandfathered, so they would not be disrupted. The measure also has broad support from firefighters, building trades, peace officers, AMVETS, and small business groups, not just billionaires. The recommendation remains NO.

The poison pill traps voters who support Prop 40 but want retirement protection. If Prop 42 receives more votes, it cancels their own vote on Prop 40.

A constitutional ban is also difficult to reverse. If a future fiscal crisis or AI-driven wealth concentration makes a carefully designed, prospective wealth tax the least-bad option, Californians would need another constitutional amendment. That high bar is the point of the measure, but it also makes broad bans costly.

The retroactivity exception is too narrow. It only covers governor-declared emergencies with revenue use limits and a 365-day lookback. Future tax legislation that needs a short transition or closes a loophole retroactively to the announcement date would be blocked. This could undermine standard anti-avoidance rules.

The fear of future middle-class retirement taxes is weak. Political incentives strongly protect 401(k)s and pensions. The pension unions supporting Prop 42 may be aligned with the billionaire PAC funding. Their support should be checked for independence. Billionaire funding does not automatically make a policy bad. Skepticism is warranted when the public justification does not match the operative effect and the primary funders' interests.

Estate taxes are typically transfer taxes rather than ownership taxes, so they likely would not be blocked. The recommendation is NO, but I am now carefully weighing the YES side to ensure a balanced analysis.

The opposition to Prop 40 is broader than billionaire PAC funding. California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, school boards, and primary care groups all oppose it. Many Democrats and healthcare organizations are against the measure. The SEIU-UHW union placed a poorly designed retroactive wealth tax on the ballot to fund its industry.

Polls showed Prop 40 was competitive, so a constitutional backstop may be the only reliable way to stop a harmful tax if voters are confused by multiple measures. Wealth taxes are almost uniformly considered bad policy by tax economists across the political spectrum.

France's wealth tax illustrates how thresholds creep downward once a tax exists. A constitutional ban is a credible commitment against that drift.

Retroactive taxation based on a pre-election residency date sets a dangerous precedent. Future initiatives could trap voters who cannot leave the state in time.

A constitutional ban on retroactive taxes is a rule-of-law protection that benefits everyone, not just billionaires. Keeping bad options open is not inherently democratic wisdom; constitutions exist precisely to take some options off the table. A stable rule against wealth-taxing middle-class savings also protects ordinary savers.

Existing taxes on vehicles and business equipment are grandfathered, so they would not be disrupted. The measure also has broad support from firefighters, building trades, peace officers, AMVETS, and small business groups, not just billionaires. The recommendation remains NO.

The poison pill traps voters who support Prop 40 but want retirement protection. If Prop 42 receives more votes, it cancels their own vote on Prop 40.

A constitutional ban is also difficult to reverse. If a future fiscal crisis or AI-driven wealth concentration makes a carefully designed, prospective wealth tax the least-bad option, Californians would need another constitutional amendment. That high bar is the point of the measure, but it also makes broad bans costly.

The retroactivity exception is too narrow. It only covers governor-declared emergencies with revenue use limits and a 365-day lookback. Future tax legislation that needs a short transition or closes a loophole retroactively to the announcement date would be blocked. Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Proposition 42 says it protects your 401(k). Who does it really protect? | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 2, 2026 3:35 PM
Prop. 42 would block new state taxes on personal property and limit retroactive taxes, challenging California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax in 2026.
Victorburnside
Getty Images/iStockphoto
The backers ofProposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) want voters to believe it is needed to prevent state legislators from raiding the retirement accounts of everyday Californians.
But the principal backers of Prop. 42 are billionaires seeking to avoid higher taxes and thwartProposition 40 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316881754.html), the controversial ballot measure that would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s richest residents.
Prop. 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html) is one of two ballot measures that could derail Prop. 40. The other isProposition 41. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html) Under the California Constitution, when two measures approved in the same election conflict, the one receiving more affirmative votes prevails. Thus, if either Prop. 42 or Prop. 41 receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the one-time 5 percent wealth tax on Californians with more than $1 billion in assets, would not take effect.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html)
At its core, Prop. 42 is presented as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts. If approved, it would bar new state taxes on those assets, though its real purpose is to shield billionaires from the tax proposed by Prop. 40.
The suggestion that any governor who would raid the modest retirement nest eggs or property of middle-class Californians is crazy because that governor would soon be unemployed for trying. Even the left-leaning state Legislature, which enjoys spending more than it should, knows not to mess with your 401(k).
Prop. 42 purports to address a problem that does not exist. It would prohibit new state taxes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on personal property—including retirement accounts, savings, investments and business interests—and restrict certain retroactive taxes. The measure would embed those limits in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them.
Even without Prop. 40 on the ballot, Prop. 42 would create the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property. In fact, it would restrict the state’s future options for taxing those assets, while a later constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure could still alter that policy.
Opponents claim that it is illegal to tax retirement accounts such as 401(k)s. This appears to be an unsettled legal issue (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/irc-403b-tax-sheltered-annuity-plans) because no government has been reckless enough to try. To assert that a constitutional amendment is necessary to protect the nest eggs of every-day Californians is beyond overreach.
Proposition 40 squarely voters with a question: Should California impose a one-timewealth tax on roughly 200 residents with net worth above $1 billion? (https://www.businessinsider.com/california-billionaires-list-wealth-tax-2026-1) Prop. 42 exists to undermine that choice and should be judged accordingly—by the interests of the billionaires financing it.
Prop. 42 is a poison pill designed to derail the real debate over a one-time wealth tax on billionaires. Voters should reject the decoy and vote no.

Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.

Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”

That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.

It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.

Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.

Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.

Proposition 42 says it protects your 401(k). Who does it really protect? | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 2, 2026 3:35 PM
Prop. 42 would block new state taxes on personal property and limit retroactive taxes, challenging California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax in 2026.
Victorburnside
Getty Images/iStockphoto
The backers ofProposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) want voters to believe it is needed to prevent state legislators from raiding the retirement accounts of everyday Californians.
But the principal backers of Prop. 42 are billionaires seeking to avoid higher taxes and thwartProposition 40 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316881754.html), the controversial ballot measure that would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s richest residents.
Prop. 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html) is one of two ballot measures that could derail Prop. 40. The other isProposition 41. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html) Under the California Constitution, when two measures approved in the same election conflict, the one receiving more affirmative votes prevails. Thus, if either Prop. 42 or Prop. 41 receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the one-time 5 percent wealth tax on Californians with more than $1 billion in assets, would not take effect.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html)
At its core, Prop. 42 is presented as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts. If approved, it would bar new state taxes on those assets, though its real purpose is to shield billionaires from the tax proposed by Prop. 40.
The suggestion that any governor who would raid the modest retirement nest eggs or property of middle-class Californians is crazy because that governor would soon be unemployed for trying. Even the left-leaning state Legislature, which enjoys spending more than it should, knows not to mess with your 401(k).
Prop. 42 purports to address a problem that does not exist. It would prohibit new state taxes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on personal property—including retirement accounts, savings, investments and business interests—and restrict certain retroactive taxes. The measure would embed those limits in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them.
Even without Prop. 40 on the ballot, Prop. 42 would create the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property. In fact, it would restrict the state’s future options for taxing those assets, while a later constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure could still alter that policy.
Opponents claim that it is illegal to tax retirement accounts such as 401(k)s. This appears to be an unsettled legal issue (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/irc-403b-tax-sheltered-annuity-plans) because no government has been reckless enough to try. To assert that a constitutional amendment is necessary to protect the nest eggs of every-day Californians is beyond overreach.
Proposition 40 squarely voters with a question: Should California impose a one-timewealth tax on roughly 200 residents with net worth above $1 billion? (https://www.businessinsider.com/california-billionaires-list-wealth-tax-2026-1) Prop. 42 exists to undermine that choice and should be judged accordingly—by the interests of the billionaires financing it.
Prop. 42 is a poison pill designed to derail the real debate over a one-time wealth tax on billionaires. Voters should reject the decoy and vote no.

Carefully reviewing the proposition details to form a recommendation.

Prop 42 would ban new state taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and personal savings starting January 1, 2026. The definition is extremely broad.

The definition covers pensions, 401(k)s, IRAs, mutual funds, and all personal property including digital assets, business interests, and intellectual property.

The proposition also prohibits retroactive taxes with limited exceptions for emergencies. Taxes in effect before December 31, 2025 remain unchanged. Real property taxation is unaffected.

Prop 42 contains a conflict clause. If it passes with more votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 is null and void entirely.

The campaign frames this as protecting middle-class retirement from double taxation. However, California currently does not tax ownership of retirement accounts or financial assets. No serious legislative proposal exists that would tax ordinary 401(k)s.

The proposition is funded by billionaire donors, including Sergey Brin, and its main purpose appears to be killing Prop 40. Major editorial boards have called it a poison pill and decoy.

Its broad definition would also constitutionally block future wealth taxes and taxes on business interests, intellectual property, digital assets, and personal belongings.

The ban would be permanent, requiring a constitutional amendment to undo it.

The retroactivity prohibition is broader than the retirement protection. It would generally bar retroactive taxes with only narrow emergency exceptions.

Prop 40 already exempts qualified retirement accounts and limits Roth conversions to $10 million. The warning about 401(k) taxes is therefore largely false.

The broad constitutional prohibition would add another rigid constraint on California's tax system. This reduces flexibility for future crises such as climate change, healthcare needs, or AI economic disruption.

The Mercury News specifically warns that the proposition would "senselessly shackles the state's fiscal future" in the face of AI-induced economic uncertainties.

Local taxes remain unaffected. Vehicle license fees and existing personal property taxes continue.

Arguments for Prop 42 independent of Prop 40 include the difficulty of valuing private businesses, art, and intellectual property. Wealth taxes would be litigation-prone. Some billionaires have already left California, suggesting capital flight.

European countries largely repealed wealth taxes due to capital flight, administrative costs, and low revenue. Taxing unrealized gains can force sales of illiquid assets. Wealth already taxed as income creates legitimate double taxation concerns. California already imposes the highest top income tax rate in the United States plus high capital gains taxes.

Prop 40 would tax people based on residency as of January 1, 2026. This is genuinely retroactive and punitive because it cannot be avoided by leaving after the measure qualifies.

Constitutional protection of savings from wealth taxation is a legitimate policy preference. Many voters reasonably do not want the state to have the power to tax asset ownership.

The slippery slope argument is not always fallacious in tax policy. Opening the door to wealth taxes could allow future expansions beyond billionaires, similar to how income tax and AMT evolved. Supporters cite six proposals targeting retirement and savings, but these claims need verification. The Orange County Register and San Bernardino Sun have endorsed YES on both propositions specifically to limit taxation.

Pension unions representing firefighters, building trades, and peace officers support Prop 42. The healthcare union SEIU-UHW supports Prop 40 instead. These pension unions fear future expansions of wealth taxes despite the current exemptions.

California's budget depends heavily on high-income taxpayers and capital gains. Blocking wealth taxes could protect that revenue base from flight.

Voting YES on Prop 42 is effectively voting to kill Prop 40. If you oppose the billionaire tax, vote directly on Prop 40 instead of allowing a misleading measure to nullify it.

The constitutional ban would also permanently block future non-retroactive wealth taxes and taxes on digital assets.

The conflict clause is especially problematic. It would void an entire competing measure, even parts that do not actually conflict with Prop 42.

A blanket constitutional ban also prevents future voters from rejecting specific bad proposals without undoing the entire tax system.

The broad definition could also block new vehicle taxes, state-level business personal property taxes, and taxes on unrealized capital gains if structured as ownership or control taxes.

The definition of "tax" in Prop 42 is drawn from Article XIII A Section 3. That section was broadened by Prop 26 in 2010 to cover any state levy, charge, or exaction. Fees that are not technically taxes may still be permitted.

The Mercury News and San Francisco Chronicle both recommend voting NO on Prop 42. I still need to verify the six retirement tax proposals and review the LAO analysis of Prop 40 before finalizing a recommendation.

The Sacramento Bee also recommends voting NO on Prop 42. The editorial consensus is largely against it, even among papers that oppose Prop 40.

I am weighing whether to rely on that consensus or form my own independent view. I generally oppose broad constitutional tax prohibitions that lock in policy beyond the specific problem. California's experience with Prop 13 offers a cautionary tale about how popular constitutional limits can create long-term structural problems.

The proposition's marketing is dishonest. It frames itself as a simple 401(k) protection, but the actual text bans ownership taxes on nearly all non-real-estate property and includes a broad retroactivity clause. A blanket constitutional ban is also too sweeping; voting no on Prop 40 would address the specific retroactive billionaire tax without destroying the state's fiscal flexibility.

The LAO analysis confirms that voting no on Prop 42 leaves the state free to consider future wealth tax proposals on their merits. It does not guarantee that such taxes will be adopted.

The fear of future middle-class retirement taxes is weak. Political incentives strongly protect 401(k)s and pensions. The pension unions supporting Prop 42 may be aligned with the billionaire PAC funding. Their support should be checked for independence. Billionaire funding does not automatically make a policy bad. Skepticism is warranted when the public justification does not match the operative effect and the primary funders' interests.

Estate taxes are typically transfer taxes rather than ownership taxes, so they likely would not be blocked. The recommendation is NO, but I am now carefully weighing the YES side to ensure a balanced analysis.

The opposition to Prop 40 is broader than billionaire PAC funding. California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, school boards, and primary care groups all oppose it. Many Democrats and healthcare organizations are against the measure. The SEIU-UHW union placed a poorly designed retroactive wealth tax on the ballot to fund its industry.

Polls showed Prop 40 was competitive, so a constitutional backstop may be the only reliable way to stop a harmful tax if voters are confused by multiple measures. Wealth taxes are almost uniformly considered bad policy by tax economists across the political spectrum.

France's wealth tax illustrates how thresholds creep downward once a tax exists. A constitutional ban is a credible commitment against that drift.

Retroactive taxation based on a pre-election residency date sets a dangerous precedent. Future initiatives could trap voters who cannot leave the state in time.

A constitutional ban on retroactive taxes is a rule-of-law protection that benefits everyone, not just billionaires. Keeping bad options open is not inherently democratic wisdom; constitutions exist precisely to take some options off the table. A stable rule against wealth-taxing middle-class savings also protects ordinary savers.

Existing taxes on vehicles and business equipment are grandfathered, so they would not be disrupted. The measure also has broad support from firefighters, building trades, peace officers, AMVETS, and small business groups, not just billionaires. The recommendation remains NO.

The poison pill traps voters who support Prop 40 but want retirement protection. If Prop 42 receives more votes, it cancels their own vote on Prop 40.

A constitutional ban is also difficult to reverse. If a future fiscal crisis or AI-driven wealth concentration makes a carefully designed, prospective wealth tax the least-bad option, Californians would need another constitutional amendment. That high bar is the point of the measure, but it also makes broad bans costly.

The retroactivity exception is too narrow. It only covers governor-declared emergencies with revenue use limits and a 365-day lookback. Future tax legislation that needs a short transition or closes a loophole retroactively to the announcement date would be blocked. This could undermine standard anti-avoidance rules.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Prop 42 papers over its real purpose by cynically appealing to middle-class worries about retirement security. Reject this appalling tactic and disincentivize its further use by voting no.

Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Policy should focus on upward mobility—better schools, safer communities, etc. - not simply equal $$
