barred, thereby cutting off the federal matching funds and supplemental payments to
nursing facilities that the program exists to generate.
Single-Subject Threats
It is also possible that Prop 41 could make it impossible for any future initiative to
be exempt from the Gann limit, yoking California to the fiscal system of the distant 1970s in
perpetuity. The California Constitution requires that an initiative “embracing more than
one subject” may not be submitted to the voters or have any effect.20 Because Proposition
41's restrictions would be added to the Constitution (if they pass), a future revenue
measure could escape the restrictions only by pairing its new tax with a constitutional
override of Proposition 41. This thus gives opponents of any future revenue measure a
powerful new tool for challenging such measures through litigation. That is, future
initiatives would have to have what are arguably two subjects: their own goals, and also
disabling the Prop 41 rules.
It might be objected in regard to this that provisions suspending Prop 41 rules that
would frustrate a future initiative are part of a single subject, much as today many
initiatives suspend the Gann limit . But would such a structure be effective? The initiative
would now both impose a tax and change the separate constitutional rule that Prop 41
added as to the Gann limit. Arguably, a court could find that these are two separate subjects
that would require two separate measures. Although California’s single-subject test is
lenient, and a combined measure could thus potentially survive challenge, even just the

Proposition 42
Proposition 42 does at least three things: 1) it offers unneeded21 protection of
retirement assets; 2) it prohibits a tax “on the ownership or control of . . . individually-
owned assets” and 3) it prohibits retroactive taxes. As with Proposition 41, though, Prop
42’s deceptive framing and sloppy language has the potential to cause great collateral
harm.

Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo IN SUMMARY Prop. 40 opponents say the billionaire tax allows lawmakers to change the measure with a two-thirds vote. They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. incomes above $1 million as a new tax because the existing additional income tax is
temporary and will not continue post-2030 unless voters remove its sunset. Notably,
Proposition 42 does not specify how its exemption clause applies to extensions of this sort.
Taxpayers thus may be able to argue that Proposition 41 prohibits the tax imposed
by Proposition 3 because the latter is a tax “on the ownership or control” of property.
Because Proposition 42 never defines “ownership or control,” its protected category
potentially encompasses all income-producing personal property; it is a longstanding
income tax principle that income from a property is taxed “to the one who controls it.” For
example, consider the current treatment of stock options one earns as part of one’s job.
Such options are treated as labor income and, if exercised years later, a formula is used to
assess how much of their appreciation should be attributed to California.22 A court might

Proposition 42 could also arguably void Proposition 3 entirely if Proposition 42 gets
more votes. Proposition 42 has a sweeping conflicts provision (Sec. 5(a)) that could be read
to trigger if Proposition 3 were interpreted as permitting any form of taxation prohibited
by Proposition 42. Note further in regard to this that California adjudicators have recently
read formal tax terms, such as “unitary business,”23 “gross receipts,”24 and “agricultural
business activity,”25 in ways the drafters of those terms plainly did not anticipate, and
“personal property” could well follow a similar pattern.26
Moreover, Proposition 42 separately prohibits a post-2025 tax that “operates
retroactively to result in tax liability based on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred
or was present prior to the effective date” of the law. Sec. 2(a)(1). A court could hold that
this clause applies where post-2030 taxes fall on gains that accrued, or on equity
compensation earned, in earlier years. If so, the post-2030 rates could not be collected with
respect to income deemed attributable to earlier years, such as gain reflecting appreciation
that accrued before 2031 or compensation from services performed earlier. This could
substantially undermine the revenue-raising capacity of Prop 3. And a ruling of this kind
would also satisfy the second trigger of Proposition 42's conflicts provision, and so (as
discussed above), could result in all of Prop 3 being nullified.

certain rigid formalism seems appealing to the California judiciary sometimes.

property but a tax on a privilege. See Ingels v. Riley, 5 Cal. 2d. 154 (1936). But Prop 42 would seem
to apply to a privilege tax.
10
the constitution, which requires the state to backfill localities if the rate falls below 0.65%
(Art. XI, Sec. 15). Given that the current rate of the VLF (0.65%) is lower than the rate that
it was long before, and the sound policy reasons why the rate should at least be the same as
the rate for real property (1%), Prop 42 will interfere with the Legislature or the people
increasing this tax. While Prop 13 doesn’t leave much room for maneuver on real estate
taxes, Proposition 42 would constrict that freedom even further by apparently prohibiting
any future state changes, absent a constitutional amendment.
Retroactivity
Prop 42’s limit on retroactive taxes will also make future tax reform harder and less
effective. Again, the only real policy payoff of this provision is to sink the billionaire tax; the
Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment of the federal constitution already bars states
from engaging in unreasonable retroactive taxation.28 In many cases good tax policy
requires that new taxes apply to at least some transactions that happened before the tax
was adopted. New taxes are often effective prior to enactment date in order to prevent
arbitrage or other evasive transactions before the tax can go into effect. Other retroactive
measures may simply fix a mistake or close off an unintended tax shelter that taxpayers
have been exploiting, as in the leading Supreme Court cases. In other cases, going back to
sometime before enactment of the tax may ensure a more accurate measure of the tax base.
For example, the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did just that.29 Having a tax change be
retroactive to the start of the year is also a way to start raising revenue immediately should
that be desired. All of these practices are longstanding and common and flow from the
states’ inherent power to control their own revenue systems.
Prop 42’s retroactivity bar could also further complicate health care financing
legislation. Provider fee statutes are sometimes written so that they apply to periods that
begin before enactment, with collection following once federal approval arrives. A post-
2025 statute with this structure could thus be threatened by Prop 42, Sec. 2(a)(1). The
existing hospital fee framework predates 2026 and thus has a grandfather defense
shielding it from these threats,30 but this defense does not protect future bills that may
reach backward, and so drafters will face new constraints and risks if Prop 42 passes.
Conclusion
California’s public finance rules are already exceptionally baroque. This irrational
opacity is particularly harmful considering that California’s underlying tax bases have not
28 United States v. Carlton, 512 U.S. 26 (1994).
29 26 USC 965(a)(1).
30 Sec. 2(b).
11
been substantially reformed for a century and the state has many urgent needs. Both
Propositions 41 and 42 add even more complexity to this rickety system, which, by itself,
should be avoided. As it is, the complicated and vague new rules that would be imposed by
Propositions 41 and 42 are likely to make it much harder to finance all manner of public
goods going forward.

might impact a variety of current taxes or those that might reasonably be proposed. For

apply to the Vehicle License Fee, which is a tax on personal property.27 This fee is so
important to local governments that it was guaranteed to them by Prop 30 (Art. XIII, Sec.
36(b)(2)) and the allocation of its revenues to local governments is protected elsewhere in

taxes, Proposition 42 would constrict that freedom even further by apparently prohibiting

Retroactivity
Prop 42’s limit on retroactive taxes will also make future tax reform harder and less
effective. Again, the only real policy payoff of this provision is to sink the billionaire tax; the
Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment of the federal constitution already bars states
from engaging in unreasonable retroactive taxation.28 In many cases good tax policy
requires that new taxes apply to at least some transactions that happened before the tax
was adopted. New taxes are often effective prior to enactment date in order to prevent
arbitrage or other evasive transactions before the tax can go into effect. Other retroactive
measures may simply fix a mistake or close off an unintended tax shelter that taxpayers
have been exploiting, as in the leading Supreme Court cases. In other cases, going back to
sometime before enactment of the tax may ensure a more accurate measure of the tax base.
For example, the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did just that.29 Having a tax change be
retroactive to the start of the year is also a way to start raising revenue immediately should
that be desired. All of these practices are longstanding and common and flow from the
states’ inherent power to control their own revenue systems.
Prop 42’s retroactivity bar could also further complicate health care financing
legislation. Provider fee statutes are sometimes written so that they apply to periods that
begin before enactment, with collection following once federal approval arrives. A post-
2025 statute with this structure could thus be threatened by Prop 42, Sec. 2(a)(1). The
existing hospital fee framework predates 2026 and thus has a grandfather defense
shielding it from these threats,30 but this defense does not protect future bills that may
reach backward, and so drafters will face new constraints and risks if Prop 42 passes.
Conclusion
California’s public finance rules are already exceptionally baroque. This irrational
opacity is particularly harmful considering that California’s underlying tax bases have not

Propositions 41 and 42 add even more complexity to this rickety system, which, by itself,
should be avoided. As it is, the complicated and vague new rules that would be imposed by
Propositions 41 and 42 are likely to make it much harder to finance all manner of public
goods going forward.

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

shields them from the effects of Prop 3. Again, Prop 3 extends the existing but temporary
1% additional income tax on incomes above $1 million, which is set to expire in 2030. Like
Proposition 41, Proposition 42 exempts taxes “in effect, imposed, and first collected” before
2026, and it is uncertain whether a court would find that Proposition 3 qualifies for that
exemption. A court might deem the permanent post-2030 additional income tax on
incomes above $1 million as a new tax because the existing additional income tax is
temporary and will not continue post-2030 unless voters remove its sunset. Notably,
Proposition 42 does not specify how its exemption clause applies to extensions of this sort.
Taxpayers thus may be able to argue that Proposition 41 prohibits the tax imposed
by Proposition 3 because the latter is a tax “on the ownership or control” of property.
Because Proposition 42 never defines “ownership or control,” its protected category
potentially encompasses all income-producing personal property; it is a longstanding
income tax principle that income from a property is taxed “to the one who controls it.” For
example, consider the current treatment of stock options one earns as part of one’s job.
Such options are treated as labor income and, if exercised years later, a formula is used to
assess how much of their appreciation should be attributed to California.22 A court might
21 California broadly conforms to the positive tax benefits given to retirement savings by the federal
tax code. See generally Ca. Rev. and Tax Code 17501 et seq. Further, any reduction in these benefits
granted by California tax law would require a 2/3 supermajority. Cal. Constit. Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
Proposition 40 does not change any of this and, in fact, explicitly exempts true retirement assets.
See Proposition 40, Proposed Section 50303(c)(7).
22 See Cal. Code Regs. tit. 18, section 17951-5(b).

treat the post-2030 taxation of that option appreciation, or even of capital gains generally,
as a tax on the ownership or control of “financial assets” that is grandfathered only through
2030.
Proposition 42 could also arguably void Proposition 3 entirely if Proposition 42 gets
more votes. Proposition 42 has a sweeping conflicts provision (Sec. 5(a)) that could be read
to trigger if Proposition 3 were interpreted as permitting any form of taxation prohibited
by Proposition 42. Note further in regard to this that California adjudicators have recently
read formal tax terms, such as “unitary business,”23 “gross receipts,”24 and “agricultural
business activity,”25 in ways the drafters of those terms plainly did not anticipate, and
“personal property” could well follow a similar pattern.26
Moreover, Proposition 42 separately prohibits a post-2025 tax that “operates
retroactively to result in tax liability based on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred
or was present prior to the effective date” of the law. Sec. 2(a)(1). A court could hold that
this clause applies where post-2030 taxes fall on gains that accrued, or on equity
compensation earned, in earlier years. If so, the post-2030 rates could not be collected with
respect to income deemed attributable to earlier years, such as gain reflecting appreciation
that accrued before 2031 or compensation from services performed earlier. This could
substantially undermine the revenue-raising capacity of Prop 3. And a ruling of this kind
would also satisfy the second trigger of Proposition 42's conflicts provision, and so (as
discussed above), could result in all of Prop 3 being nullified.
Other Taxes
Proposition 42’s restrictions as to the taxation of other assets are very broad and
might impact a variety of current taxes or those that might reasonably be proposed. For
example, consider the bar on taxing “personal property.” This would, on its face, seem to
apply to the Vehicle License Fee, which is a tax on personal property.27 This fee is so
important to local governments that it was guaranteed to them by Prop 30 (Art. XIII, Sec.
36(b)(2)) and the allocation of its revenues to local governments is protected elsewhere in

the constitution, which requires the state to backfill localities if the rate falls below 0.65%
(Art. XI, Sec. 15). Given that the current rate of the VLF (0.65%) is lower than the rate that
it was long before, and the sound policy reasons why the rate should at least be the same as
the rate for real property (1%), Prop 42 will interfere with the Legislature or the people
increasing this tax. While Prop 13 doesn’t leave much room for maneuver on real estate
taxes, Proposition 42 would constrict that freedom even further by apparently prohibiting
any future state changes, absent a constitutional amendment.
Retroactivity
Prop 42’s limit on retroactive taxes will also make future tax reform harder and less
effective. Again, the only real policy payoff of this provision is to sink the billionaire tax; the
Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment of the federal constitution already bars states
from engaging in unreasonable retroactive taxation.28 In many cases good tax policy
requires that new taxes apply to at least some transactions that happened before the tax
was adopted. New taxes are often effective prior to enactment date in order to prevent
arbitrage or other evasive transactions before the tax can go into effect. Other retroactive
measures may simply fix a mistake or close off an unintended tax shelter that taxpayers
have been exploiting, as in the leading Supreme Court cases. In other cases, going back to
sometime before enactment of the tax may ensure a more accurate measure of the tax base.
For example, the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did just that.29 Having a tax change be
retroactive to the start of the year is also a way to start raising revenue immediately should
that be desired. All of these practices are longstanding and common and flow from the
states’ inherent power to control their own revenue systems.
Prop 42’s retroactivity bar could also further complicate health care financing
legislation. Provider fee statutes are sometimes written so that they apply to periods that
begin before enactment, with collection following once federal approval arrives. A post-
2025 statute with this structure could thus be threatened by Prop 42, Sec. 2(a)(1). The
existing hospital fee framework predates 2026 and thus has a grandfather defense
shielding it from these threats,30 but this defense does not protect future bills that may
reach backward, and so drafters will face new constraints and risks if Prop 42 passes.
Conclusion
California’s public finance rules are already exceptionally baroque. This irrational
opacity is particularly harmful considering that California’s underlying tax bases have not

30 Sec. 2(b).

been substantially reformed for a century and the state has many urgent needs. Both
Propositions 41 and 42 add even more complexity to this rickety system, which, by itself,
should be avoided. As it is, the complicated and vague new rules that would be imposed by
Propositions 41 and 42 are likely to make it much harder to finance all manner of public
goods going forward.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Research is complete. I will answer yes or no.

The answer is no. The proposition would ban new state taxes on personal property and most retroactive taxes, and nullify conflicting measures like Prop 40.

A no vote does not impose any tax. It simply preserves the state's option to tax ownership of financial assets.

The proposition's sales pitch is misleading. California does not tax ownership of retirement accounts. Prop 40 already exempts qualified pensions and most retirement accounts.

The proposition is a billionaire-backed kill switch, not a retirement protection act. Building a Better California spent over $150 million on Yes on 42, funded by Sergey Brin, John Doerr, and Eric Schmidt. The legal text explicitly nullifies Prop 40 if it passes. The retroactivity ban is custom-drafted to target Prop 40's January 1, 2026 hook. Wealth-tax bills have died in the legislature since 2019.

The constitutional lock-in is too broad. It would cover all personal property, business interests, and digital assets, not just retirement accounts. Undoing it would require another constitutional amendment. California already has a dense web of fiscal constraints like Prop 13 and Gann. Adding poorly drafted ones creates litigation risk. Tax scholars warn that disputes could arise over capital gains, VLF reform, and anti-avoidance effective dates.

The retroactivity ban is broader than the problem it targets. Due process already limits retroactive taxes. A blanket ban with only a 365-day emergency exception would block standard anti-avoidance and year-start effective dates. That creates real governance costs for a provision whose sole purpose is killing one ballot measure.

The case for yes is weak. Wealth taxes are poor policy, but a broad constitutional ban is worse. The state can reject specific proposals without embedding a deceptive lock-in. Rewarding poison-pill tactics would encourage more of them.

The argument that a constitutional ban protects the tax base from flight is weak. Billionaires who left over Prop 40 already did so; a constitutional lock-in would not bring them back if Prop 40 fails on its own.

Editorial coverage reveals a clear split. Newspapers that oppose both the wealth tax and the countermeasures — including the Mercury News, East Bay Times, SF Chronicle, and Sacramento Bee — take the more careful position: do not use a bad instrument to stop a bad tax.

Papers that support the proposition — including OCR, Press-Enterprise, and U-T — are anti-tax outlets that would back almost any tax limitation. The governance argument against it is stronger than the ideological argument for it. Polls show a plurality now oppose both Prop 41 and Prop 42, which undermines the "protect your 401k" message once voters learn more.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.

SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West

PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.
It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.

Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property's value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
Proposal
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more "yes" votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effect
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
Ballot Label

‘Billionaire tax’ Prop 40 and its rival props 41 and 42
We dive deep into Prop 40 and its rival props, 41 and 42, and what's at stake.
Under Proposition 42, the state would not be able to institute any new taxes on personal property, including retirement accounts, other than real estate. It would also prevent most new taxes from being applied retroactively.
Understanding Prop. 42
Proposition 42 is partly an effort to block another measure voters will see on their ballot, Proposition 40 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax). Also known as the billionaire’s tax, Proposition 40 seeks to establish a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires in California. (You can read more about Proposition 40 here (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax).)
Proposition 42 would effectively kill Proposition 40, even if both measures pass: If Proposition 42 gets more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaire’s tax could be declared void, according to an analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm) from the California Secretary of State.
For example, under Proposition 40, a billionaire subject to the tax would have to pay based on their accumulated wealth, including wealth from their intellectual property and artwork and jewelry they have in the state. Proposition 42 would make it so such assets cannot be taxed.
Official title on the ballot: Prohibits new state personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) :
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
Sponsored message
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A "no" vote means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
Here's what supporters say
California's high cost of living and taxes have made living in the state difficult, and Proposition 42 aims to put a cap on any attempt to go further. For example: California’s constitution currently allows for taxes on things people own, such as art on display in a home, that haven't generated any taxable revenue. Proposition 42 would block such taxes.
Notable endorsements: Los Angeles and Orange Counties Building and Construction Trades Council; California Professional Firefighters; California Society of Certified Public Accountants; several business groups, including the Valley Industry and Commerce Association and Greater Los Angeles African American Chamber of Commerce.
Here's what opponents say
They criticize Proposition 42 for shielding billionaires from paying a one-time tax to help stabilize the healthcare system in California.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party; SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West; supporters of Proposition 40.
Potential financial impact
The California Secretary of State’s analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm) found that, if approved, Proposition 42 could make it harder for the state to raise taxes in the future: “This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.”
What it takes to win
A majority is needed to pass.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> California voters in November will determine the fate of potential new taxes in more than one way.
Proposition 42 is described as an effort to protect retirement and personal savings, but it’s also among two measures that could block a proposed billionaire tax intended to primarily fund healthcare.
Called the Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act, it would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes.
Advertisement

Oct. 1, 2026
What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. That includes financial assets, investment accounts, intellectual property, personal belongings and other assets used for retirement or financial planning.
It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, because the two measures conflict with each other. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Proposition 42 could reduce state tax revenue but it’s unclear by how much, according to the office’s analysis. Currently, the state does tax certain personal property such as vehicles. It doesn’t tax people for owning financial assets like stocks and investment accounts but does tax income from them.
How much they have raised
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Advertisement
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Small Business Assn., California Senior Alliance, California Professional Firefighters and other groups back the measure.
“Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California — we need protection against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings,” supporters wrote in favor of the measure.
More than $73 million has been contributed to support Proposition 42 with the vast majority coming from Building a Better California. Google co-founder Sergey Brin, venture capitalists and other tech executives fund that group.
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> A powerful labor union backing the billionaire tax is fighting Proposition 42 and another proposition that could cancel out its measure even if voters approve that too.
“Don’t be fooled — Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes,” Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, wrote in arguments against the proposition. “It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.”

Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The measure states that its purpose is to protect Californians’ ability to save for retirement and the future, though opponents say it’s meant to trick voters into canceling the billionaire tax.

conflicting initiative measure approved by the voters at

later held invalid, this measure shall be self-executing

SEC. 2. Findings and Declarations.
(a) California families are paying more for everything
and we already pay some of the highest taxes in the
country. A recent analysis by a nonpartisan research
institute concluded that California ranks 3rd worst in
the nation in subjecting its population to taxes when
considering individual income taxes, sales taxes,
property taxes, and other forms of taxation. California is
behind only New Jersey and the District of Columbia in
this regard. California also has the highest state sales

tax in the nation, the highest top income tax rate, and
the highest tax on gasoline, among other indicators.
(b) Every day, Californians are also facing an
affordability crisis. Costs for housing, food, electricity,
health care, home and auto insurance, and many other
life necessities continue to escalate. Californians are
struggling economically just to make ends meet on a
daily basis. Saving for retirement or a rainy day is even
harder. Given the state’s extraordinarily high cost of
living, a recent analysis suggests that Californians
would need $2.3 million saved up if they want to retire
comfortably for 20 years. This is an impossible sum for
many Californians.
(c) To make matters worse, politicians and special
interest groups want to start taxing retirement holdings,
individually owned assets, and other forms of personal
savings—even though the “California Dream” is getting
further out of reach for many of us and many
Californians struggle to save enough money to retire.
Here is just some of what could be at risk:
(1) Teachers, police officers, firefighters, and other
dedicated workers earn defined-benefit pension
benefits. They could be taxed on the future value of
their pension benefits and forced to pay the
government before they ever collect a dime in pension
pay.
(2) Californians who contribute to 401(k) retirement
plans and individual retirement accounts (IRAs), and
invest in stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and other
investments could be taxed on the value of their
retirement nest eggs. This could cost workers some of
their hard-earned savings, causing them to put off
retirement and leaving them more economically
vulnerable later in life.
(d) California already imposes income taxes, capital
gains taxes, real property taxes, personal property
taxes, corporation taxes, sales and use taxes, real
property transaction taxes and many other taxes on its
residents. In addition, once Californians begin to
access their retirement holdings, sell their individually
owned assets, or realize the growth in other personal
savings, they are already subject to the state’s income,
capital gains, and property taxes. But politicians and
special interests should be prohibited from taxing the
mere ownership or control of personal property such as
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings that Californians work
hard to save.
(e) Retroactive taxes can have the same devastating
effects on Californians’ retirement planning and
personal savings. Fundamental principles of fairness in
a democratic society require that individuals, families,
and businesses be able to understand and rely upon
the tax laws that govern their financial planning so they
can make decisions with advance notice of what the
rules are.
(f) The ability of Californians to organize and achieve
their financial and retirement goals depends on having
advance notice of the tax obligations that apply to
them. Retroactive changes to tax laws are
fundamentally unfair and undermine confidence in
government, disrupt retirement and financial planning,
and prevent residents and businesses from preparing
for the future.
(g) Sacramento politicians and special interests have
wasted billions of our tax dollars on inefficient and
ineffective programs. But they keep coming back for
more of our money with more tax proposals. They don’t
need to tax our retirement holdings or tax us
retroactively based on past conduct, activities, or
status—they need to deliver better results with what
taxpayers have already given them to spend.

people of the State of California is to protect
Californians’ ability to save for their futures by
prohibiting the imposition of new taxes on our personal
property, including the ownership or control of
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings as well as requiring all
new taxes to only apply prospectively.

Carefully reviewing the proposition details to form a recommendation.

Prop 42 would ban new state taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and personal savings starting January 1, 2026. The definition is extremely broad.

The definition covers pensions, 401(k)s, IRAs, mutual funds, and all personal property including digital assets, business interests, and intellectual property.

The proposition also prohibits retroactive taxes with limited exceptions for emergencies. Taxes in effect before December 31, 2025 remain unchanged. Real property taxation is unaffected.

Prop 42 contains a conflict clause. If it passes with more votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 is null and void entirely.

The campaign frames this as protecting middle-class retirement from double taxation. However, California currently does not tax ownership of retirement accounts or financial assets. No serious legislative proposal exists that would tax ordinary 401(k)s.

The proposition is funded by billionaire donors, including Sergey Brin, and its main purpose appears to be killing Prop 40. Major editorial boards have called it a poison pill and decoy.

Its broad definition would also constitutionally block future wealth taxes and taxes on business interests, intellectual property, digital assets, and personal belongings.

The ban would be permanent, requiring a constitutional amendment to undo it.

The retroactivity prohibition is broader than the retirement protection. It would generally bar retroactive taxes with only narrow emergency exceptions.

Prop 40 already exempts qualified retirement accounts and limits Roth conversions to $10 million. The warning about 401(k) taxes is therefore largely false.

The broad constitutional prohibition would add another rigid constraint on California's tax system. This reduces flexibility for future crises such as climate change, healthcare needs, or AI economic disruption.

The Mercury News specifically warns that the proposition would "senselessly shackles the state's fiscal future" in the face of AI-induced economic uncertainties.

Local taxes remain unaffected. Vehicle license fees and existing personal property taxes continue.

Arguments for Prop 42 independent of Prop 40 include the difficulty of valuing private businesses, art, and intellectual property. Wealth taxes would be litigation-prone. Some billionaires have already left California, suggesting capital flight.

European countries largely repealed wealth taxes due to capital flight, administrative costs, and low revenue. Taxing unrealized gains can force sales of illiquid assets. Wealth already taxed as income creates legitimate double taxation concerns. California already imposes the highest top income tax rate in the United States plus high capital gains taxes.

Prop 40 would tax people based on residency as of January 1, 2026. This is genuinely retroactive and punitive because it cannot be avoided by leaving after the measure qualifies.

Constitutional protection of savings from wealth taxation is a legitimate policy preference. Many voters reasonably do not want the state to have the power to tax asset ownership.

The slippery slope argument is not always fallacious in tax policy. Opening the door to wealth taxes could allow future expansions beyond billionaires, similar to how income tax and AMT evolved. Supporters cite six proposals targeting retirement and savings, but these claims need verification. The Orange County Register and San Bernardino Sun have endorsed YES on both propositions specifically to limit taxation.

Pension unions representing firefighters, building trades, and peace officers support Prop 42. The healthcare union SEIU-UHW supports Prop 40 instead. These pension unions fear future expansions of wealth taxes despite the current exemptions.

California's budget depends heavily on high-income taxpayers and capital gains. Blocking wealth taxes could protect that revenue base from flight.

Voting YES on Prop 42 is effectively voting to kill Prop 40. If you oppose the billionaire tax, vote directly on Prop 40 instead of allowing a misleading measure to nullify it.

The constitutional ban would also permanently block future non-retroactive wealth taxes and taxes on digital assets.

The conflict clause is especially problematic. It would void an entire competing measure, even parts that do not actually conflict with Prop 42.

A blanket constitutional ban also prevents future voters from rejecting specific bad proposals without undoing the entire tax system.

The broad definition could also block new vehicle taxes, state-level business personal property taxes, and taxes on unrealized capital gains if structured as ownership or control taxes.

The definition of "tax" in Prop 42 is drawn from Article XIII A Section 3. That section was broadened by Prop 26 in 2010 to cover any state levy, charge, or exaction. Fees that are not technically taxes may still be permitted.

The Mercury News and San Francisco Chronicle both recommend voting NO on Prop 42. I still need to verify the six retirement tax proposals and review the LAO analysis of Prop 40 before finalizing a recommendation.

The Sacramento Bee also recommends voting NO on Prop 42. The editorial consensus is largely against it, even among papers that oppose Prop 40.

I am weighing whether to rely on that consensus or form my own independent view. I generally oppose broad constitutional tax prohibitions that lock in policy beyond the specific problem. California's experience with Prop 13 offers a cautionary tale about how popular constitutional limits can create long-term structural problems.

The proposition's marketing is dishonest. It frames itself as a simple 401(k) protection, but the actual text bans ownership taxes on nearly all non-real-estate property and includes a broad retroactivity clause. A blanket constitutional ban is also too sweeping; voting no on Prop 40 would address the specific retroactive billionaire tax without destroying the state's fiscal flexibility.

The LAO analysis confirms that voting no on Prop 42 leaves the state free to consider future wealth tax proposals on their merits. It does not guarantee that such taxes will be adopted.

The fear of future middle-class retirement taxes is weak. Political incentives strongly protect 401(k)s and pensions. The pension unions supporting Prop 42 may be aligned with the billionaire PAC funding. Their support should be checked for independence. Billionaire funding does not automatically make a policy bad. Skepticism is warranted when the public justification does not match the operative effect and the primary funders' interests.

Estate taxes are typically transfer taxes rather than ownership taxes, so they likely would not be blocked. The recommendation is NO, but I am now carefully weighing the YES side to ensure a balanced analysis.

The opposition to Prop 40 is broader than billionaire PAC funding. California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, school boards, and primary care groups all oppose it. Many Democrats and healthcare organizations are against the measure. The SEIU-UHW union placed a poorly designed retroactive wealth tax on the ballot to fund its industry.

Polls showed Prop 40 was competitive, so a constitutional backstop may be the only reliable way to stop a harmful tax if voters are confused by multiple measures. Wealth taxes are almost uniformly considered bad policy by tax economists across the political spectrum.

France's wealth tax illustrates how thresholds creep downward once a tax exists. A constitutional ban is a credible commitment against that drift.

Retroactive taxation based on a pre-election residency date sets a dangerous precedent. Future initiatives could trap voters who cannot leave the state in time.

A constitutional ban on retroactive taxes is a rule-of-law protection that benefits everyone, not just billionaires. Keeping bad options open is not inherently democratic wisdom; constitutions exist precisely to take some options off the table. A stable rule against wealth-taxing middle-class savings also protects ordinary savers.

Existing taxes on vehicles and business equipment are grandfathered, so they would not be disrupted. The measure also has broad support from firefighters, building trades, peace officers, AMVETS, and small business groups, not just billionaires. The recommendation remains NO.

The poison pill traps voters who support Prop 40 but want retirement protection. If Prop 42 receives more votes, it cancels their own vote on Prop 40.

A constitutional ban is also difficult to reverse. If a future fiscal crisis or AI-driven wealth concentration makes a carefully designed, prospective wealth tax the least-bad option, Californians would need another constitutional amendment. That high bar is the point of the measure, but it also makes broad bans costly.

The retroactivity exception is too narrow. It only covers governor-declared emergencies with revenue use limits and a 365-day lookback. Future tax legislation that needs a short transition or closes a loophole retroactively to the announcement date would be blocked. This could undermine standard anti-avoidance rules.

Estate taxes are typically transfer taxes rather than ownership taxes, so they likely would not be blocked. The recommendation is NO, but I am now carefully weighing the YES side to ensure a balanced analysis.

The opposition to Prop 40 is broader than billionaire PAC funding. California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, school boards, and primary care groups all oppose it. Many Democrats and healthcare organizations are against the measure. The SEIU-UHW union placed a poorly designed retroactive wealth tax on the ballot to fund its industry.

Polls showed Prop 40 was competitive, so a constitutional backstop may be the only reliable way to stop a harmful tax if voters are confused by multiple measures. Wealth taxes are almost uniformly considered bad policy by tax economists across the political spectrum.

France's wealth tax illustrates how thresholds creep downward once a tax exists. A constitutional ban is a credible commitment against that drift.

Retroactive taxation based on a pre-election residency date sets a dangerous precedent. Future initiatives could trap voters who cannot leave the state in time.

A constitutional ban on retroactive taxes is a rule-of-law protection that benefits everyone, not just billionaires. Keeping bad options open is not inherently democratic wisdom; constitutions exist precisely to take some options off the table. A stable rule against wealth-taxing middle-class savings also protects ordinary savers.

Existing taxes on vehicles and business equipment are grandfathered, so they would not be disrupted. The measure also has broad support from firefighters, building trades, peace officers, AMVETS, and small business groups, not just billionaires. The recommendation remains NO.

The poison pill traps voters who support Prop 40 but want retirement protection. If Prop 42 receives more votes, it cancels their own vote on Prop 40.

A constitutional ban is also difficult to reverse. If a future fiscal crisis or AI-driven wealth concentration makes a carefully designed, prospective wealth tax the least-bad option, Californians would need another constitutional amendment. That high bar is the point of the measure, but it also makes broad bans costly.

The retroactivity exception is too narrow. It only covers governor-declared emergencies with revenue use limits and a 365-day lookback. Future tax legislation that needs a short transition or closes a loophole retroactively to the announcement date would be blocked. Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.
