Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.

Proposition 42 says it protects your 401(k). Who does it really protect? | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 2, 2026 3:35 PM
Prop. 42 would block new state taxes on personal property and limit retroactive taxes, challenging California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax in 2026.
Victorburnside
Getty Images/iStockphoto
The backers ofProposition 42 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) want voters to believe it is needed to prevent state legislators from raiding the retirement accounts of everyday Californians.
But the principal backers of Prop. 42 are billionaires seeking to avoid higher taxes and thwartProposition 40 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316881754.html), the controversial ballot measure that would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s richest residents.
Prop. 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html) is one of two ballot measures that could derail Prop. 40. The other isProposition 41. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317122476.html) Under the California Constitution, when two measures approved in the same election conflict, the one receiving more affirmative votes prevails. Thus, if either Prop. 42 or Prop. 41 receives more yes votes than Prop. 40, the one-time 5 percent wealth tax on Californians with more than $1 billion in assets, would not take effect.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 42 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317007039.html)
At its core, Prop. 42 is presented as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts. If approved, it would bar new state taxes on those assets, though its real purpose is to shield billionaires from the tax proposed by Prop. 40.
The suggestion that any governor who would raid the modest retirement nest eggs or property of middle-class Californians is crazy because that governor would soon be unemployed for trying. Even the left-leaning state Legislature, which enjoys spending more than it should, knows not to mess with your 401(k).
Prop. 42 purports to address a problem that does not exist. It would prohibit new state taxes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on personal property—including retirement accounts, savings, investments and business interests—and restrict certain retroactive taxes. The measure would embed those limits in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them.
Even without Prop. 40 on the ballot, Prop. 42 would create the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property. In fact, it would restrict the state’s future options for taxing those assets, while a later constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure could still alter that policy.
Opponents claim that it is illegal to tax retirement accounts such as 401(k)s. This appears to be an unsettled legal issue (https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/irc-403b-tax-sheltered-annuity-plans) because no government has been reckless enough to try. To assert that a constitutional amendment is necessary to protect the nest eggs of every-day Californians is beyond overreach.
Proposition 40 squarely voters with a question: Should California impose a one-timewealth tax on roughly 200 residents with net worth above $1 billion? (https://www.businessinsider.com/california-billionaires-list-wealth-tax-2026-1) Prop. 42 exists to undermine that choice and should be judged accordingly—by the interests of the billionaires financing it.
Prop. 42 is a poison pill designed to derail the real debate over a one-time wealth tax on billionaires. Voters should reject the decoy and vote no.

In summary
California voters haven’t had to make so many decisions about tax policy at the ballot since 1990. Our analysis shows voters tend to reject new taxes.

California voters will soon be asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And they’ll be asked whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They’ll also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.

Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

PROP 42: The Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-09/California%20Decides_Proposition%2042.pdf)

Overview
Key Questions
Analysis & Assessment
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Proposition 42 would add a new article to the California Constitution with two main provisions:
First, it would prohibit any new taxes on personal property—both tangible (i.e., personal belongings) and intangible (savings, retirement accounts, financial assets, business ownership, intellectual property, etc.)—while leaving existing property taxes untouched. In effect, this would require that the California legislature get voters’ approval before creating any new property taxes.
Second, it would prohibit new taxes that impose liability for past residency or conduct, with a narrow exception allowing taxes to reach back up to 365 days if tied to a governor-declared emergency and dedicated to addressing it.
Notably, if Prop 42 gets more votes than Proposition 40, it would nullify Prop 40 entirely. Given the two propositions fundamentally conflict, this kind of specificity is valuable to clearly determine what happens after the election. This is arguably the most relevant element of Prop 42, because Prop 40 could possibly allow future legislators to pass new taxes on personal property.
Fellows at the Hoover Institution have extensively researched (https://fiscalrealitycheck.substack.com/p/a-california-ballot-collision-wealth) Prop 40, Prop 42, and California’s fiscal problems more generally. The biggest fiscal challenge the state faces is an exuberance of spending beyond what even its rapidly increasing tax revenue can sustain.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0041A1)
Type: Initiated constitutional amendment and statute
A vote YES means: A prohibition on new state taxes on personal property, including financial assets. Retroactive taxes would be prohibited except during a state of emergency. If Proposition 42 outpolls Proposition 40, it would specifically void Prop 40 (see California Decides Proposition Lab, Prop 40: The Billionaire Tax Act (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-40)).
A vote NO means: The legislature would not be forbidden from passing new taxes on personal property, including financial assets. The legislature would not be forbidden from passing retroactive taxes. The lack of these restrictions is especially relevant if Proposition 40 passes, because Prop 40 arguably empowers future legislatures to pass new taxes on personal property and to create retroactive taxes.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0041A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0041A1%20(Retirement%20Protection%20).pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0041 (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250545.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 40 imposes a one-time tax of 5 percent on the total net worth of any California resident worth $1 billion or more. The rate applies to the whole fortune, not just the amount above the threshold. A narrow phase-in ramps the rate between 0 percent at $1.0 billion and 5 percent at $1.1 billion. A married couple is treated as a single taxpayer.
Residency is set as of January 1, 2026, called the tax obligation date, and net worth is measured on December 31, 2026, called the valuation date. The January date is already in the past. A billionaire who leaves California before the election would still owe the tax if voters approve it because the law reaches back to who lived here on the first day of the year. The tax is due in 2027 with 2026 tax returns, payable in full or in five annual installments that carry a 7.5 percent additional charge each year.
Not all assets are included in the net worth calculation. Directly held real estate is excluded, which sidesteps a fight with Proposition 13 restrictions. Pensions and traditional retirement accounts are excluded, Roth accounts are excluded up to $10 million, and up to $5 million of art, cars, and personal property is excluded.
The revenue from this tax is not allowed to go into the general fund. The constitutional amendment routes it into a separate reserve fund that sits outside the Gann appropriations limit, the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee, and the rainy-day budget rules. The revenue is earmarked: 90 percent goes to healthcare and 10 percent to education and food assistance, with annual spending caps of $22.5 billion and $2.5 billion. This provision reaches every taxpayer in the state: All 19 million-plus California income tax filers would have to declare whether their net worth exceeds $1 billion.
2. The legal language
Full text:
Initiative 25-0041A1, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0041A1%20(Retirement%20Protection%20).pdf) (six pages, amended language filed January 12, 2026)
Key language:
“No state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026 may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether held directly or indirectly.”
What it amends:
Adds a new Article VIII to the California Constitution. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal it, and only another vote of the people can undo it. The measure borrows the definition of “tax” from Article XIII A, Section 3, the Proposition 13 and Proposition 26 definition. It also includes a conflicting-measures clause that reaches other initiatives on the same ballot.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
A constitutional ban on new taxes on the ownership or control of personal property, from personal belongings and savings (including retirement accounts) to business interests and intellectual property. It would also prohibit most new retroactive state taxes, including taxes keyed to a past residency date.
Where?
Statewide, written into the state constitution.
When?
It would apply to taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026.
Why?
The proponents say California already ranks among the most heavily taxed states, that families struggle to save, and that politicians should not be able to tax the value of savings and assets people have already earned.
4. Analysis and Assessment
Proposition 42 would prohibit the legislature from enacting future taxes on personal property, broadly defined. This would be a negligible change to the status quo because the state does not currently levy taxes on tangible or intangible personal property. However, it would forestall future legislatures from taxing personal property without first getting approval from voters via ballot initiative.
The California Constitution currently permits the legislature, with a two-thirds vote, to levy taxes on all tangible and intangible personal property. The first sentence of Article XIII, Section 2, reads:
The Legislature may provide for property taxation of all forms of tangible personal property, shares of capital stock, evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest therein not exempt under any other provision of this article.
This language reflects dormant tax policy going back to the 1879 California Constitution. In the 1930s, after years of controversy and litigation over taxes on intangible assets and a sharp decrease in property tax revenues caused by delinquencies during the Great Depression, the state pivoted to implement a sales tax and a personal income tax to stabilize state tax revenue. As part of the tax policy coordination, a 1933 constitutional amendment retained the language allowing the state to tax personal property but limited taxes on many financial assets to be at most 0.4 percent of the value of the asset. Today, California’s Revenue and Taxation Code exempts all intangible assets from taxation. However, the income from intangible assets like stocks and debt instruments is taxed as ordinary income.
One argument against limiting what the legislature can tax is that the state’s tax base is already narrowly dependent on personal income taxes (see California Decides FAQ: Who Pays for California’s State Budget, and What Is It Spent On? (https://www.hoover.org/research/who-pays-californias-state-budget-and-what-it-spent)). The personal income tax has grown to provide nearly 70 percent (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2026-01-27/california-budget-deficit-surplus-spending-commitments) of General Fund tax revenue, compared to 38 percent for total state tax collections nationally. Research by Hoover Institution fellows Lanhee J. Chen, Lee Ohanian, and Joshua D. Rauh have described how this causes substantial volatility in the California state budget (https://www.hoover.org/research/california-state-budget-and-revenue-volatility-fiscal-health-deficit-context) because most personal income tax revenue comes from high-income and high-net-worth households and tends to fluctuate with stock market performance. For example:
During the strong stock market returns in 2021 the top 10 percent of taxpayers paid almost 90 percent of personal income tax revenue.
The top 1 percent of income tax filers typically pay 40–50 percent of personal income tax revenue.
The top 0.1 percent—just twenty-five thousand households—typically pay more than 20 percent of all personal income tax revenue.
The problem with adding new state personal property taxes, especially on intangible financial assets, is that the impact will tend to be borne by the high-income and high-net-worth households. This means that creating new property taxes wouldn’t expand the tax base—it would simply be tapping the same source of revenue that California already utilizes more than almost any other state.
Dr. Rauh’s California-specific research examining taxpayers’ response to Proposition 30 (2012) shows that high-income and high-net-worth households exhibit the highest migration response to increased taxes, meaning that new state property taxes would potentially undermine the already-precarious tax base. The departure of a significant portion of the tax base for Proposition 40’s wealth tax, even before the tax is even in effect (https://libertylensecon.substack.com/p/california-wealth-tax-npv), provides further evidence of the sensitivity of high-income and high-net-worth taxpayers to increased tax rates.
On the other hand, Proposition 42 would provide a credible commitment that the state would not create new property taxes, perhaps providing some degree of reassurance for the households most susceptible to migration, such that more will remain in the state than otherwise. That wouldn’t necessarily expand the tax base, but it would at least help prevent further erosion. Prop 42’s prohibition on retroactive taxes would likely have a similar effect.
A more relevant solution to California’s financial woes would be budget reductions to counter the recent spending explosion, as well as better management of its existing revenue streams to weather the lean times. Research by Dr. Ohanian highlights that from 2019 to 2023 California’s population declined by almost five hundred thousand people (a 1 percent decrease), but the state budget increased by more than 57 percent (31 percent after adjusting for inflation).
State personal income tax revenues surged by 55 percent in 2021 due to a soaring stock market and federal support during COVID-19, but this was followed by a 35 percent drop in 2023. The bust should have been expected given California’s previous experience, but Governor Newsom’s administration assumed that the increased revenue would be permanent and increased government spending commensurately, leading to a $175 billion swing (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2026-01-27/california-budget-deficit-surplus-spending-commitments) from budget surplus to deficit just two years later.
The boom-bust nature of California’s tax revenue shows the need for better methods to smooth revenues and spending over time. In particular, this will require restraining state policymakers, who have shown a proclivity for pursuing large projects and program expansions during the boom times, only to discover during the bust that discretion is the better part of spending. A comprehensive solution would require extensive tax structure reforms, but in the meantime state policymakers could reduce volatility by revisiting California’s “rainy day fund” to ensure it is fit for purpose.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 42 doesn’t change any current taxes. It effectively only adds the requirement that voters be consulted before the state creates any new property taxes. It also prohibits retroactive taxes and taxes keyed to a past residency date. This provides high-income and high-net-worth households a credible signal that California will not—without reasonable warning—tax the ownership of personal property, especially financial assets. This could help slow the out-migration that erodes the state’s narrow, top-heavy tax base.
Prop 42 also contains a clause that if it outpolls Proposition 40, it will fully nullify Prop 40. This specificity is likely preferrable to having the courts attempt to determine which elements of Prop 40 (if any) still hold if Prop 42 has greater support.
Hoover Institution research shows that California’s spending has risen far faster than inflation or population growth, and even faster than the surprising increases in tax revenue. This suggests that first California should solve its expenditures problem before trying to backfill tax revenue by tapping those households already responsible for the vast majority of income tax revenue.
Learn More About California
Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.

Document Type
Article

9-2026
Abstract
This memorandum discusses the possible collateral damage that Propositions 41 and 42 (on the ballot in California on November 3, 2026) might cause. The two propositions were concocted very quickly by billionaires in order to trick voters that will vote for Proposition 40 (the billionaire tax) also to vote for these propositions that are designed to undermine the billionaire tax.
The basic trick is that these propositions have plausible seeming veneers but hide a poison pill that aims to frustrate the functioning of the billionaire tax. The veneers are “plausible seeming” because they address problems that are not problems. For example, Prop 42 protects retirement assets when there is no threat to them – certainly not from Prop 40 (which exempts them).
But this memo focuses on an issue other than their deceptiveness and general disrespect for the democratic process. Because these propositions were drafted so quickly and poorly as poison pills for one tax measure, they could, if passed, impact many other vital policy initiatives. Some possible negative impacts include.
· The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could hamstring Proposition 3 (the teacher-sponsored measure to fund education with taxes on million-dollar earners) or invalidate it outright.
· The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could similarly hamstring many other revenue raising measures, such as (for example) a tax on large employers who have many employees on Medi-Cal.
· The limitations on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could impact the ability of the state to tax capital gains income, whether as part of Proposition 3 or otherwise.
· The limitation on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could frustrate any future attempt to reform California’s Vehicle License Fee, a backbone tool for financing a wide array of local services.

Checking the Gamage PDF to assess whether the collateral damage claims are serious or speculative.

Also reviewing the LA Times editorial and CalMatters fact check on expanding billionaire tax to everyone. Hoover's analysis is more favorable to Prop 42 but does not explicitly recommend voting yes. It notes negligible change to the status quo, prevents future personal property taxes without voter approval, and provides a useful conflict clause. However, it also points out that California's tax base is already narrow and dependent on high earners, so adding property taxes would not expand revenue.

Hoover's claim that the proposal only requires voter consultation is misleading. A constitutional prohibition would prevent the legislature from acting even with a two-thirds majority. Future property taxes would require a constitutional amendment, which is a higher bar than simply consulting voters. It remains unclear whether voters would approve such an amendment.

A future constitutional amendment could override Prop 42 if it explicitly repeals or conflicts with it. Voters would not be permanently locked out. The legislature would still be blocked from acting. This creates a moderate constraint rather than a permanent ban on democracy.

The argument that the proposal shackles future generations is somewhat overstated. Future voters could still override it through a constitutional amendment.

The real costs are higher barriers to change and the immediate nullification of Prop 40.

The Gamage memo claims the proposal could impact capital gains taxation. Capital gains tax is levied on the realization event rather than ownership, so it likely falls outside the proposed prohibition. The retroactivity provision would instead affect timing of income tax changes. The campaign itself may also be misleading.

Analysis of the Impacts of Propositions 41 and 42 on CaliforniaAnalysis of the Impacts of Propositions 41 and 42 on California
Public FinancePublic Finance
David Gamage
Brian D. Galle
Darien Shanske
Follow this and additional works at: https://scholarship.law.missouri.edu/facpubs
Part of the Taxation-State and Local Commons, and the Tax Law Commons
Memorandum
To: Interested Parties
From: Brian Galle (UC Berkeley), David Gamage (University of Missouri), and Darien
Shanske (UC Davis)1
Re: Analysis of the Impacts of Propositions 41 and 42 on California’s Public Finance
Date: August 20, 2026
Introduction
In this memorandum, we will discuss the potential impacts of Propositions 41 and
42 on current and future initiatives and legislation, as well as on current California
Medicaid tax programs, starting with possible impacts on Proposition 3, the measure on
November’s ballot to extend personal income tax rate increases.
The purpose of the memo is to identify legal risks raised by the propositions that
prudent citizens should be aware of given the high stakes. We are not arguing how a court
should decide these issues and we do not claim that we are offering the best or most
persuasive legal arguments. We do, however, believe that there is a real risk courts could
reach these outcomes.
Our bottom line is that both propositions are poorly drafted in a manner that could
pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key
spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises. That is not
surprising. These are deceptive measures that were drafted quickly to trick voters that
support the billionaire wealth tax (Prop 40) into voting for competing measures that could
undermine that tax. The billionaire funders of these initiatives are acting with reckless
disregard for the collateral damage to California’s fiscal system and indeed they may even
benefit from weakening California’s existing taxes affecting the most wealthy.
Executive Summary
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could hamstring Proposition 3 (the
teacher-sponsored measure to fund education with taxes on million-dollar earners)
or invalidate it outright.
1 Institutional affiliations are listed for identification purposes only.
2
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could similarly hamstring many other
revenue raising measures, such as (for example) a tax on large employers who have
many employees on Medi-Cal.
• The prohibition on easing the state appropriation limit in Proposition 41 could
undermine many existing and proposed taxes to fund California’s contributions to
Medi-Cal, including current MCO taxes and the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee
(HQAF).
• The limitations on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could impact the
ability of the state to tax capital gains income, whether as part of Proposition 3 or
otherwise.
• The limitation on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could frustrate any
future attempt to reform California’s Vehicle License Fee, a backbone tool for
financing a wide array of local services.
Proposition 41
Proposition 41 makes two significant changes to California law. First, it adds many
new audit requirements, specifically pre-election audits of programs that would receive
funds from a proposed special tax initiative; and recurring audits, every four years, of
programs receiving moneys from special taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026,
whether enacted by the Legislature or by initiative.2 Second, the proposition prohibits
collecting any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026 that is exempted
or excluded from the appropriations limit of Article XIIIB, the so-called Gann limit, whether
the exemption comes from an outside-the-General-Fund special fund whose spending is
not counted or from raising the limit itself. Proposition 41, secs. 3, 4(b). The obvious point
of this second change, hidden deep in the Proposition 41 text, is to nullify Proposition 40.
But both changes would likely weaken California public finance by threatening California’s
ability to raise revenues and fund spending programs.
On the Merits
Prop 41 targets the primary (and, in many cases, the only plausible remaining) way
that state tax policy can be done and that state services can be adequately funded. Any
increase in taxes enacted by the Legislature requires a two-thirds supermajority of each
house.3 Statewide initiatives, by contrast, can raise taxes by majority vote. Not surprisingly,
most major tax policy changes over recent decades have therefore occurred via initiative.
Since voters are unlikely to support tax increases for unspecified purposes, the limits on
2 Prop. 41, Secs. 1, 2.
3 Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
3
measures adopting taxes for specified purposes tilts the deck against most of those
measures. Even if there were eventually an attempt to change Prop 41 through another
ballot measure, the pre-election audit requirement would still apply to any special tax
initiatives on that ballot.
The audits that Prop 41 would impose are slanted to make it more difficult to adopt
and fund new programs. Consider, for example, that a pre-election audit must consider:
“How the program's costs compare to any analogous programs in the non-government
sector”; and also: “Recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary
savings of at least 10% annually.” The audits would thus institutionalize a cost-cutting,
private-sector-comparison framework, and the executive summary of the pre-election
audit would be printed in the voter guide immediately after the Legislative Analyst’s
impartial analysis.4
In sum, every proposed special tax initiative would come before the voters bundled
with an official analysis oriented toward finding savings and private alternatives. These
expensive, burdensome and largely redundant5 requirements would hinder special tax
initiatives, making them more difficult to pass and less effective if passed.
The second provision regarding the Gann limit would double down on what has
proven to be a disastrous set of fiscal policies. The existing Gann limit works by capping
government expenditures over a given two-year period. Excess amounts must be split
between taxpayer rebates and education.6 The cap increases only to the extent of growth in
California population and cost of living.7 Given the increasing demands on the state
government, future uncertainties, and the changing nature of federal assistance, the limit
does not act so much as a ceiling as a vise squeezing out funds for core services.8 For
example, what happens if the state government needs to spend more on (say) wildfires? Or,
4 Sec. 1(e)(2).
5 California law is already full of audit requirements and indeed has a powerful and independent
state auditor (Govt Code 8543 et seq, see especially GC 8546.1) that issues regular,
https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/, and, often critical, reports about state operations. See, e.g.,
https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/reponses-2025-108-all/. And sometimes the state requires
particular audits. See, e.g., Bus. And Prof. Code 6145(b). As further discussed, the income tax
extensions authorized by Proposition 3 are already subject to audit. Art. XIII, Sec. 36(g).
6 Art. XIIIB, Sec. 2.
7 Art. XIIIB, Secs. 8(e), (f).
8 Making a similar point, here is Jason Sisney (an Assembly budget insider): “Therefore, if revenues
push the state to its Gann limit, non-Proposition 98 programmatic spending (such as annual tax-
supported spending on health and human services (HHS), housing, universities, prisons, state
employees and natural resources programs) probably would have to be cut more in this situation.”
https://jasonsisney.substack.com/p/state-moving-closer-to-its-appropriation
4
what if the state government must spend more to backfill vicious cuts from the federal
government?
The state has hit the Gann limit recently (2022) and is about $30 billion under the
Gann limit currently. Suppose Prop 3 passes without incident and the AI boom does lead to
substantial increases in revenue. At that point, the state will be close to the limit. Any
possible new initiatives for education, child care, housing or wildfire abatement could then
well go over the limit.
Threats to Proposition 3
The audit requirements of Proposition 41 arguably apply to Proposition 3 because
Proposition 3 would seem to impose a “special tax” enacted “by a statewide initiative
measure on or after January 1, 2026.” Sec. 2(a)(1). Proposition 3 makes permanent the
existing 1% tax surcharge on income above $1 million that is set to expire in 2030; all of its
revenues are earmarked primarily for education. It thus likely involves a “special tax,”
which is “a tax that can only be used to fund specific, as opposed to unlimited, purposes”
(according to Prop 41), because the Education Protection Account revenues added by Prop
3 may be used only for specified education and health care purposes. Sec. 4(d) of
Proposition 41; Article XIII, Sec. 36(e) of Proposition 3.
As for whether Proposition 3 was enacted after January 1, 2026, a court could
plausibly find that a tax first approved in 2012 is “enacted” in 2026 when the voters delete
its sunset. The new provision is different than the old in that it will never expire; the post-
2030 tax will exist only because of the 2026 vote; and the adoption of the extension is itself
literally an enactment.9
Thus, Proposition 41 might plausibly be interpreted by courts as applying to
Proposition 3. If so, Proposition 41 would require onerous and burdensome audits of the
programs it funds.
Further, if both measures pass and Proposition 41 receives more affirmative votes,
every provision of Proposition 3, including the rate extension itself, could be ruled void.
The terms of Proposition 41 state that it nullifies other conflicting 2026 initiatives if it
receives more votes. Prop 41 defines conflicting measures as “another initiative measure
9 Notably, neither Prop 41’s prohibition nor its grandfather clause discusses extensions, even
though California drafters know how to address extensions expressly. For instance, Proposition 218
reaches taxes that governments “impose, extend, or increase,” and the Proposition 218
implementation statute treats removal of a sunset as an extension. Art. XIII C, Sec. 2(b); Gov. Code
Sec. 53750(e).
5
that …imposes different audit rules on special taxes.” Sec. 5(a). Proposition 3 carries
forward Proposition 30’s audit rules, and those rules are different from Proposition 41’s.10
Threats to the MCO Tax
The sloppy drafting of Proposition 41 implicates policies far beyond Proposition 3.
We will briefly consider spending on health care.
Start with the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax, which California expects to
generate as much as $8 billion annually in federal matching funds. There are now arguably
two separate MCO provisions that will take effect after 2026 authorization, both of them
threatened by Prop 41.
The first is SB 125, enacted in June 2026, which imposes a tax of $8.85 per enrollee
per month for 2027 through 2029 and deposits the proceeds in the new Medi-Cal Stability
Fund, dedicated to specified Medi-Cal purposes.11 SB 125 is a special tax enacted after
January 1, 2026, so under Prop 41 each Medi-Cal program receiving its moneys would face
recurring State Auditor financial and performance audits, with the private-sector
comparisons and ten percent savings recommendations, and with the Auditor reimbursed
from the tax revenues themselves.12 As explained above, this would be very burdensome
and problematic. And because the Stability Fund broadly co-funds managed care payments
and rates, there is a further risk that a court would rule that the auditable “programs”
include major portions of Medi-Cal managed care, rather than just the marginal SB 125
dollars. Thus Prop 41 could require the state to pay for audits recommending how to
privatize Medi-Cal and slash it by 10%.
Proposition 41 also deprives the state of flexibility to keep SB 125 effective in the
future. As enacted, the SB 125 tax uses up capacity under the Gann limit, narrowing room
for other revenue needs. SB 125 also sunsets in 2030, at a time when there might not be
room under the Gann limit available for renewal. In both cases, the state could be left
choosing between crowding out other priorities under the limit or losing the tax—and the
10 Indeed, on one point the two measures give seemingly incompatible commands about the same
dollars. Proposition 41 provides that the State Auditor “shall be reimbursed from the revenue
generated by the special tax” for the reasonable costs of its audits. Sec. 2(d). Section 36 (Proposition
3), however, provides that moneys deposited in the Education Protection Account for education
“shall not be used to pay any costs incurred by the Legislature, the Governor, or any agency of state
government,” and it separately bars using Account funds for administrative costs. Art. XIII, Sec.
36(e)(5), (6).
11 Ch. 24, Stats. 2026 (SB 125), adding a new Article 7.2 to the Welfare and Institutions Code; the
new tax is expressly made not subject to Proposition 35's chapter. See Dept. of Finance, Manual of
State Funds, Fund 3492 (Medi-Cal Stability Fund classified as included).
12 Sec. 2.
6
federal matching grants it secures— altogether. This would of course have major negative
implications for state funding of Medi-Cal.
In addition, in 2024, Proposition 35 implemented a permanent MCO tax starting in
2027.13 Proposition 35 also used a provision of the Gann limit, Art. XIIIB, Sec. 4, to lift the
ceiling for four years in order to accommodate the new spending.14 Recall that Prop 41
prohibits collecting any tax that modifies the Gann limit if the tax takes effect on or after
January 1, 2026. 15 There is thus a significant risk Prop 41 would prevent Proposition 35
from taking effect.
Threats to the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee (HQAF)
Prop 41 could also bar modifications to the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee (HQAF),
including modifications that might be required by the federal government in order for the
HQAF to remain in effect. The HQAF draws down billions of dollars in federal matching
funds for hospital payments, and the federal government approved the 2025 program in
June 2026. HQAF funds are exempt from the Gann limit.16 A court might conclude that an
HQAF modified after January 1, 2026 “takes effect” after that date for purposes of Prop 41.
That would prevent California from modifying or improving the HQAF, even if required by
federal rule changes, such as those now pending. A Trump or other hostile HHS aware of
this dilemma might go out of its way to require HQAF changes that it knows California
cannot implement.17
We expect that California would argue the HQAF is not subject to Prop 41 limits
because it is a “fee,” not a “tax,” but a court might well rule otherwise. This is because
Proposition 41 does not define “state tax” and because California generally interprets
“taxes” quite broadly. See Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(b). A multibillion dollar charge that funds not
only services for the payors but also transfers to others, as the HQAF does, will be quite
likely to face a plausible challenge that it constitutes a tax and not a fee.
Note that the stakes of these threats are further magnified because the statute
makes it so that the hospital fee becomes inoperative if a lawsuit is filed and a preliminary
13 Welf. & Inst. Code § 14199.123(b).
14 Proposition 35, Sec. 2.
15 Prop. 41, Secs. 3, 4(b)(2).
16 Cal. Const., art. XVI, § 3.5(d); Dept. of Finance, Manual of State Funds (Hospital Quality Assurance
Revenue Fund classified as excluded from the state appropriations limit). The Finance fund record
predates Proposition 52 and is based on the notion that the revenues are not proceeds of taxes;
Proposition 52 is the source of the constitutional exclusion.
17 It could also be argued that the HQAF takes effect after Jan. 1, 2026 even if it is not modified after
that date. This is because its mechanics operate through discrete, numbered program periods, and
each of these has its own fee model and its own federal approval. Thus, a period beginning after
January 1, 2026 could well be characterized as the tax taking effect after that date.
7
injunction or other order results in a loss of federal financial participation or any net
General Fund cost.18 A qualifying preliminary injunction or other order could thus obstruct
the program well before any final judgment, even if the challenge might ultimately fail on
the merits.
Threats to the Skilled Nursing Facility Fees
Yet another health funding source at risk from Proposition 41 is the skilled nursing
facility quality assurance fee (SNF-QAF). Like the HQAF, this is a provision intended to
generate federal matching funds, and it is expected to bring in several billion dollars over
the next 5 years. The SNF-QAF was extended by the Legislature in July 2026 through the
end of 2027,19 and its revenues are also classified as exempt from the Gann limit. Thus, a
court could well decide based on these arguments that collection of the fee should be
barred, thereby cutting off the federal matching funds and supplemental payments to
nursing facilities that the program exists to generate.
Single-Subject Threats
It is also possible that Prop 41 could make it impossible for any future initiative to
be exempt from the Gann limit, yoking California to the fiscal system of the distant 1970s in
perpetuity. The California Constitution requires that an initiative “embracing more than
one subject” may not be submitted to the voters or have any effect.20 Because Proposition
41's restrictions would be added to the Constitution (if they pass), a future revenue
measure could escape the restrictions only by pairing its new tax with a constitutional
override of Proposition 41. This thus gives opponents of any future revenue measure a
powerful new tool for challenging such measures through litigation. That is, future
initiatives would have to have what are arguably two subjects: their own goals, and also
disabling the Prop 41 rules.
It might be objected in regard to this that provisions suspending Prop 41 rules that
would frustrate a future initiative are part of a single subject, much as today many
initiatives suspend the Gann limit . But would such a structure be effective? The initiative
would now both impose a tax and change the separate constitutional rule that Prop 41
added as to the Gann limit. Arguably, a court could find that these are two separate subjects
that would require two separate measures. Although California’s single-subject test is
lenient, and a combined measure could thus potentially survive challenge, even just the
18 Welf. & Inst. Code § 14169.72.
19 SB 165, signed July 6, 2026; see Dept. of Finance, Manual of State Funds, Fund 3213 (Long-Term
Care Quality Assurance Fund classified as excluded).
20 Art. II, Sec. 8(d).

They warn it opens the door to future wealth taxes on everyday Californians. This is only partially true. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. s will likely argue that it
shields them from the effects of Prop 3. Again, Prop 3 extends the existing but temporary
1% additional income tax on incomes above $1 million, which is set to expire in 2030. Like
Proposition 41, Proposition 42 exempts taxes “in effect, imposed, and first collected” before
2026, and it is uncertain whether a court would find that Proposition 3 qualifies for that
exemption. A court might deem the permanent post-2030 additional income tax on
incomes above $1 million as a new tax because the existing additional income tax is
temporary and will not continue post-2030 unless voters remove its sunset. Notably,
Proposition 42 does not specify how its exemption clause applies to extensions of this sort.
Taxpayers thus may be able to argue that Proposition 41 prohibits the tax imposed
by Proposition 3 because the latter is a tax “on the ownership or control” of property.
Because Proposition 42 never defines “ownership or control,” its protected category
potentially encompasses all income-producing personal property; it is a longstanding
income tax principle that income from a property is taxed “to the one who controls it.” For
example, consider the current treatment of stock options one earns as part of one’s job.
Such options are treated as labor income and, if exercised years later, a formula is used to
assess how much of their appreciation should be attributed to California.22 A court might
21 California broadly conforms to the positive tax benefits given to retirement savings by the federal
tax code. See generally Ca. Rev. and Tax Code 17501 et seq. Further, any reduction in these benefits
granted by California tax law would require a 2/3 supermajority. Cal. Constit. Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
Proposition 40 does not change any of this and, in fact, explicitly exempts true retirement assets.
See Proposition 40, Proposed Section 50303(c)(7).
22 See Cal. Code Regs. tit. 18, section 17951-5(b).
9
treat the post-2030 taxation of that option appreciation, or even of capital gains generally,
as a tax on the ownership or control of “financial assets” that is grandfathered only through
2030.
Proposition 42 could also arguably void Proposition 3 entirely if Proposition 42 gets
more votes. Proposition 42 has a sweeping conflicts provision (Sec. 5(a)) that could be read
to trigger if Proposition 3 were interpreted as permitting any form of taxation prohibited
by Proposition 42. Note further in regard to this that California adjudicators have recently
read formal tax terms, such as “unitary business,”23 “gross receipts,”24 and “agricultural
business activity,”25 in ways the drafters of those terms plainly did not anticipate, and
“personal property” could well follow a similar pattern.26
Moreover, Proposition 42 separately prohibits a post-2025 tax that “operates
retroactively to result in tax liability based on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred
or was present prior to the effective date” of the law. Sec. 2(a)(1). A court could hold that
this clause applies where post-2030 taxes fall on gains that accrued, or on equity
compensation earned, in earlier years. If so, the post-2030 rates could not be collected with
respect to income deemed attributable to earlier years, such as gain reflecting appreciation
that accrued before 2031 or compensation from services performed earlier. This could
substantially undermine the revenue-raising capacity of Prop 3. And a ruling of this kind
would also satisfy the second trigger of Proposition 42's conflicts provision, and so (as
discussed above), could result in all of Prop 3 being nullified.
Other Taxes
Proposition 42’s restrictions as to the taxation of other assets are very broad and
might impact a variety of current taxes or those that might reasonably be proposed. For
example, consider the bar on taxing “personal property.” This would, on its face, seem to
apply to the Vehicle License Fee, which is a tax on personal property.27 This fee is so
important to local governments that it was guaranteed to them by Prop 30 (Art. XIII, Sec.
36(b)(2)) and the allocation of its revenues to local governments is protected elsewhere in
23 Garcia-Rojas et al. v. Franchise Tax Board, A172054 (Cal. Ct. App. May 1, 2026).
24 Appeal of Microsoft Corp. and Subsidiaries, 2024-OTA-130 (Cal. Off. Tax App. July 27, 2023).
25 Smithfield Packaged Meats Corp. v. California Franchise Tax Board, No. 21STCV39637 (Cal. Super.
Ct. 2026) (final statement of decision).
26 We do not mean to imply here that we agree with these decisions, but the fact remains that a
certain rigid formalism seems appealing to the California judiciary sometimes.
27 Now, there is some complexity here because the VLF was held in 1936 not to be a tax on personal
property but a tax on a privilege. See Ingels v. Riley, 5 Cal. 2d. 154 (1936). But Prop 42 would seem
to apply to a privilege tax.
10
the constitution, which requires the state to backfill localities if the rate falls below 0.65%
(Art. XI, Sec. 15). Given that the current rate of the VLF (0.65%) is lower than the rate that
it was long before, and the sound policy reasons why the rate should at least be the same as
the rate for real property (1%), Prop 42 will interfere with the Legislature or the people
increasing this tax. While Prop 13 doesn’t leave much room for maneuver on real estate
taxes, Proposition 42 would constrict that freedom even further by apparently prohibiting
any future state changes, absent a constitutional amendment.
Retroactivity
Prop 42’s limit on retroactive taxes will also make future tax reform harder and less
effective. Again, the only real policy payoff of this provision is to sink the billionaire tax; the
Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment of the federal constitution already bars states
from engaging in unreasonable retroactive taxation.28 In many cases good tax policy
requires that new taxes apply to at least some transactions that happened before the tax
was adopted. New taxes are often effective prior to enactment date in order to prevent
arbitrage or other evasive transactions before the tax can go into effect. Other retroactive
measures may simply fix a mistake or close off an unintended tax shelter that taxpayers
have been exploiting, as in the leading Supreme Court cases. In other cases, going back to
sometime before enactment of the tax may ensure a more accurate measure of the tax base.
For example, the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act did just that.29 Having a tax change be
retroactive to the start of the year is also a way to start raising revenue immediately should
that be desired. All of these practices are longstanding and common and flow from the
states’ inherent power to control their own revenue systems.
Prop 42’s retroactivity bar could also further complicate health care financing
legislation. Provider fee statutes are sometimes written so that they apply to periods that
begin before enactment, with collection following once federal approval arrives. A post-
2025 statute with this structure could thus be threatened by Prop 42, Sec. 2(a)(1). The
existing hospital fee framework predates 2026 and thus has a grandfather defense
shielding it from these threats,30 but this defense does not protect future bills that may
reach backward, and so drafters will face new constraints and risks if Prop 42 passes.
Conclusion
California’s public finance rules are already exceptionally baroque. This irrational
opacity is particularly harmful considering that California’s underlying tax bases have not
28 United States v. Carlton, 512 U.S. 26 (1994).
29 26 USC 965(a)(1).
30 Sec. 2(b).
11
been substantially reformed for a century and the state has many urgent needs. Both
Propositions 41 and 42 add even more complexity to this rickety system, which, by itself,
should be avoided. As it is, the complicated and vague new rules that would be imposed by
Propositions 41 and 42 are likely to make it much harder to finance all manner of public
goods going forward.

Research is complete. I will answer yes or no.

The answer is no. The proposition would ban new state taxes on personal property and most retroactive taxes, and nullify conflicting measures like Prop 40.

A no vote does not impose any tax. It simply preserves the state's option to tax ownership of financial assets.

The proposition's sales pitch is misleading. California does not tax ownership of retirement accounts. Prop 40 already exempts qualified pensions and most retirement accounts.

The proposition is a billionaire-backed kill switch, not a retirement protection act. Building a Better California spent over $150 million on Yes on 42, funded by Sergey Brin, John Doerr, and Eric Schmidt. The legal text explicitly nullifies Prop 40 if it passes. The retroactivity ban is custom-drafted to target Prop 40's January 1, 2026 hook. Wealth-tax bills have died in the legislature since 2019.

The constitutional lock-in is too broad. It would cover all personal property, business interests, and digital assets, not just retirement accounts. Undoing it would require another constitutional amendment. California already has a dense web of fiscal constraints like Prop 13 and Gann. Adding poorly drafted ones creates litigation risk. Tax scholars warn that disputes could arise over capital gains, VLF reform, and anti-avoidance effective dates.

The retroactivity ban is broader than the problem it targets. Due process already limits retroactive taxes. A blanket ban with only a 365-day emergency exception would block standard anti-avoidance and year-start effective dates. That creates real governance costs for a provision whose sole purpose is killing one ballot measure.

The case for yes is weak. Wealth taxes are poor policy, but a broad constitutional ban is worse. The state can reject specific proposals without embedding a deceptive lock-in. Rewarding poison-pill tactics would encourage more of them.

The argument that a constitutional ban protects the tax base from flight is weak. Billionaires who left over Prop 40 already did so; a constitutional lock-in would not bring them back if Prop 40 fails on its own.

Editorial coverage reveals a clear split. Newspapers that oppose both the wealth tax and the countermeasures — including the Mercury News, East Bay Times, SF Chronicle, and Sacramento Bee — take the more careful position: do not use a bad instrument to stop a bad tax.

Papers that support the proposition — including OCR, Press-Enterprise, and U-T — are anti-tax outlets that would back almost any tax limitation. The governance argument against it is stronger than the ideological argument for it. Polls show a plurality now oppose both Prop 41 and Prop 42, which undermines the "protect your 401k" message once voters learn more.
